News.title: Mobbed by crowds, Trump talk & beer… on the campaign trail with Nigel Farage as he rallies ‘Brexit Army’ to stop Starmer
News.content:
IS Nigel Farage the Messiah or just a very naughty boy?

His fans here in Yorkshire certainly mob him with an almost God-like reverence as he tours the towns and villages.





“They come up to me, grab my hands and say, ‘Save us’,” the Reform leader tells me.

But does destiny really call for Farage — or is that just the beer talking?

We are well into our day on the campaign trail — and a few cheeky pints to the good — by the time I sit down with him for a chat at Barnsley social club.

The relationship between Farage and his supporters is in many ways an unlikely one.

What business does a posh former City trader, wearing an expensive linen suit, have preaching to an old mining community?

They may be cut from different cloth, but these are his voters now.

To them, Farage is their “last hope” of stopping Britain spiralling into an irreversible decline.



To him, they are his “People’s Army”, first marshalled in their millions to vote for Brexit.

Now he hopes to rally them again to turf Sir Keir Starmer out of No10.

It was during that 2016 referendum campaign where Labour’s Red Wall first started to show signs of cracking, before imploding completely three years later under Jeremy Corbyn.

The message from traditional working-class heartlands should have hit the Westminster establishment like a freight train.

But how do these communities see Brexit ten years on?



“Disappointed, very, very disappointed with a lack of delivery,” says Farage.

“There is deep disappointment that the realistic expectations of Brexit were not delivered by a Conservative government, and are now being reversed by a Labour government.”

So why is Farage so quiet on Brexit these days?

The man who almost single-handedly dragged Britain out of the EU often seems reluctant to talk about it.

“In the minds of most folk, it’s done, it’s over,” he says.



“It’s not been done properly.”

“But Starmer is now completely breaking his manifesto promises, and linking us to a group of economies who, in some cases, are doing even worse than we are.

“So the whole thing is madness, and we’ll fight.

“We won’t call it Brexit.

“But we’ll fight for the principles of making our own laws in our own country, including the ability to deport people.



“Because the unfinished, completely unfinished bit of Brexit was they never even contemplated the European Convention on Human Rights.”

The ECHR is the new bogeyman of Brexiteers and those on the Right.

In many ways it is far more intrusive and damaging than the EU itself.

Farage is adamant this is the next fight: “Don’t underestimate this.

“ECHR is the new Brexit debate.



“And it sounds all very technical.

“But I promise you, knock on doors in Barnsley, they know what the ECHR is. They really do.”

That is largely because of the ECHR’s role in thwarting migrant deportations.

In recent years it has been weaponised by lawyers to such a ridiculous extent that one Albanian criminal dodged removal partly by claiming his son does not like foreign chicken nuggets.

Immigration is still a totemic issue for Reform, and as long as the boats keep coming, then one can imagine the party capitalising on it at the next election.



But what if Farage has met his match in current Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, who is looking to neutralise the Channel crisis once and for all?

“Well, we’ll order champagne for the whole room,” he says.

“But it isn’t going to happen.



“Not a cat’s chance in hell.”

He does, however, talk rather highly of Mahmood for having the guts to push through some tough migration reforms past her squeamish Labour MPs.

“I think to stand up in the face of a Labour parliamentary party that is moving quite rapidly to the left, and to say what she said, takes some courage.”

Farage also thinks Labour is charging left to blunt the threat from the Greens and that it is a mistake.

He says: “The 2024 voters who’ve deserted Labour, far more have come to Reform than have gone to the Greens.”



Recent polling appears to prove his point.

But that does not mean the Greens, under new leader Zack Polanski, are not also hoovering up disaffected Labour voters.

At next month’s local elections, Farage is on course to win big, with a projected 1,278 more councillors in England.

Reform is also locked in a two-horse race with Plaid Cymru in Wales and is fighting for second in Scotland.

Labour and the Tories are once again expected to bleed support as the two-party system seems in its death throes.



The traditional parties gobbled up 80 per cent of the vote just five years ago, but 2025 polls saw them plunge to their lowest ever share of just 57 per cent.

Farage may have done more than any man alive to upend that political order, but Polanski is also knocking at the door.

Is the rise of these insurgents two sides of the same coin?

Are they fishing in the same pool of disaffected working-class communities?

Farage gives the idea short shrift: “I don’t see the Green vote as being working people.



“I see the Green vote as being ethnic minorities.

“Many who don’t speak English.

“Many who have foreign passports, but are still allowed to vote, for reasons that are totally beyond me.”

In the meet-and-great with his council candidates, Farage even tells them not to bother knocking on doors during the day because people “not working are not going to vote for us”.

He is framing the May 7 local elections as a referendum on Starmer’s premiership.



“Vote Reform, Get Starmer Out” is his slogan.

Many people here in Yorkshire do not need convincing that the PM is woefully underperforming, but what can Reform councils offer them?

Reform councils have in fact been accused of promising lower council tax but actually raising it instead.

Farage responds: “I’m not promising to wave the magic wand.

“I didn’t last year either.



“I’ve never over-promised, for fear of under-delivering.

“And I can stand there and say, on the basis of the ten authorities that we run, we have delivered lower council tax rises.

“Now, I’m hoping, with those councils, over the course of the next few years, to deliver a lot more.”

Farage knows he is a Marmite figure and he is not trying to please everyone.

One thing that puts off some voters is his closeness to Donald Trump.



But the pair have been growing apart for some time now.

Farage tells me he has “left it a little bit because it’s awkward” for both men, given he is now leading a major opposition party.

He tells Trump-sceptics in Britain: “You’re not voting on President Trump.

“You’re voting on who ultimately is going to lead this country.”

Yet there is no denying the pair have similarities.



They shoot from the hip and do not care if people balk.

Farage certainly still loves pounding pavements, in part because it must be the mother of all ego boosts as people pour out of shops and pubs to get a selfie — only interrupted by the odd heckle of critics calling him a racist.

“I actually like real people, you know?” he says.

“This is now the seventh week on the road.

“And sure we get some abuse.



“We get some people shout things.

“I don’t care.

“Who I’m really interested to meet are those who haven’t quite made their minds up yet.”

As we part, I ask if he is perhaps the most famous man in Britain.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I’m not famous,” he tells me.



“I’m infamous.”

News.title: Gemma Collins’ foghorning doom loop thrives on sympathy from thick, gullible men… so I’m A Celeb was the perfect show
News.content:
OF all the disturbing incidents on I’m A Celeb: South Africa, none has troubled me more than the depth charge Scarlett Moffatt dropped at the waterfall pool earlier this week.

“Did you know,” she started, innocently enough.





“Gemma Collins has a designer vagina?”

I did not.

But now you mention it, “designed by who?” was my first thought.

Was it the same team who did Preston bus station’s renovations?

Or was it a Blue Peter competition, with Princess Michael of Kent picking the winner?

We’ll probably never know as events have moved incredibly quickly on this second series of I’m A Celeb: South Africa, which has entertained me far more than I thought possible.

For that surprising state of affairs, I think you can blame lady luck which the ITV spin-off show has enjoyed in abundance.

Foghorning loop

The first stroke was the timing.





I’m A Celeb hasn’t quite existed in a complete television vacuum, but try finding anything decent to watch this week and you’ll quickly realise it’s nearly always the least worst option at 9pm.

ITV will probably claim the second big slice involved a lot of careful planning.

Personally, I don’t buy it, but couldn’t deny that the bookers assembled an unfathomably dense and combustible bunch of exhibitionists who, if nothing else, were always likely to provide a very satisfying hate-watch.

When discussing the line-up, it’s hard, of course, to see past Gemma Collins, or indeed around her.

She is a 24/7 nightmare who seems to spend her entire life very noisily trying to quit something: Bushtucker trials, eating challenges, diets, unsuitable men, TV shows, her entire persona.

Gemma can’t wait to get out of all of them, but is now trapped inside her own self-destructive, foghorning loop for ever.

It’s a process that involves a lot of self-pity and manipulation and she seems to have developed a happy knack of getting sympathy from thick, gullible men, who weren’t exactly in short supply inside that camp.

This was the remarkable thing about IAC:SA, though.

As hard as she tried, Gemma Collins still wasn’t half as newsworthy or unpleasant as that Bluto-ish bully David Haye, or anything like as mouthy and selfish as Jimmy Bullard who was quite prepared to end Adam Thomas’s stint on the show just because he didn’t fancy his chances on Rancid Run.

The repercussions of that explosion rumble on and with so many tiresome egomaniacs and outright gits chasing the camera for almost the entire duration, I’m A Celeb could very swiftly have become unbearable.



The final stroke of luck, though, was booking the perfect celebrity antidote in the shape of Harry Redknapp who, whether Gemma, David and Jimmy have noticed or not, is living proof that you can be both famous and well-liked by the public, just by being sweet-natured and comfortable in your own skin.

Harry also has a very enviable and innocent ability to make people laugh and provided my personal highlight of the series when it was his turn to kick someone off the show.

For there are humiliating exits and then there’s Harry Redknapp telling Seann Walsh: “Stuart, I’ve had to make a decision and I’ve chosen you.”

In a just and sane TV universe, Harry will win I’m A Celeb’s live vote tonight.

Huge problem

Even if he doesn’t, though, he’s helped create an issue with I’m A Celeb: South Africa which hasn’t just been a lot better than the last series of I’m A Celebrity . . . Get Me Out Of Here!, it’s been better than most series of the increasingly feeble Australian version.

If the spin-off had as many viewers, ITV wouldn’t have such an obvious headache.

But it’s probably got just enough (four million) for the network to plough on with two series a year that will continue to eat away at demand until there’s nothing left of either of them.

How ITV solves a huge problem it’s created for itself?

I’m not 100 per cent sure, just as I’m still a bit in the dark about Gemma’s operation, although she did release one more staggering piece of information at the waterfall.

It took “only 40 minutes”.



Yet six years later, HS2 was still working on the Chiltern tunnel.

Galling.

GABBY IN CLAP TRAP

BBC1 propaganda show Have I Got News For You deserves a smidgen of sympathy, for once.

The “red flag” story about Peter Mandelson broke fairly late last Thursday, so it was given only 32 seconds air time on Friday’s episode.

This doesn’t, of course, erase the nasty suspicion Ian Hislop will deliver a “more-in-sorrow-than-in-anger” lecture instead of clearing the decks for a five-way pummelling on tonight’s show, as would’ve happened if Boris Johnson had been Prime Minister instead of Keir Starmer.

Nor does it excuse the fact Friday’s HIGNFY built its opening ten minutes around the result of Hungary’s recent elections, which would have been of no interest to 99.99 per cent of the British public.

A decision taken, of course, because the defeat of right-wing Viktor Orban appealed to the political prejudices of all the panellists, the BBC and the whooping and jeering (but rarely laughing) studio audience, who seem to set the threatening tone for everything that now happens on this hopelessly compromised show.

So pathetically desperate, in fact, is everyone to get their woke clap of approval, host Gabby Logan was prepared to spin history when panellist Michelle Wolf asked: “England’s never won a major football trophy, right?”

“Well, England haven’t won a major trophy in the men’s department,” replied Gabby.

“But the ladies’ department is doing very well.”



(Clap clap clap)

News which appealed to the twisted Tartan Army side of me, obviously.

And yet . . . with all the good grace I have at my disposal, I can’t help but think there may have been another significant football game, not long before Scotland became World Champions in 1967.

YOU’VE all heard of a Neighbourhood Watch area, right?

Advance warning about Graham Norton’s new ITV show.

It’s The Neighbourhood don’t watch area.

Unexpected morons in the bagging area

THE Finish Line, Roman Kemp: “Which city in the West Midlands is home to the Barber Institute of Fine Arts?”

Nkechi: “Scotland.”

The Weakest Link, Romesh Ranganathan: “Which word for an item of footwear sounds like a type of pastry used to make profiteroles?”

Jordan Gray: “Cake.”



And Romesh: “In TV, the phrase ‘Winter is coming’, first spoken by Ned Stark, is from which fantasy drama series?”

Ella Thomas: “Friends.”

Random TV irritations

GRACE DENT’S MasterChef voice going “the full Exorcist” every time she attempts to sound sultry.

Paul Merton trying to hijack everyone else’s jokes on Have I Got News For You.

All-mouth-and-no-trousers Jimmy Bullard bottling out of I’m A Celeb: South Africa. Alex Scott and other woke BBC cretins killing off 52-year-old Football Focus.

And a brief cameo from Mr Blobby highlighting the fact that he was not just Claudia Winkleman’s funniest chat show guest but, rather damningly, her most famous and likeable one as well.

Great sporting insights

PAUL MERSON: “Man City are usually always Man City.”

Ian Holloway: “They’ve got to handle the pressure because there isn’t any.”

Liam Rosenior: “We’ll have a chat when we’re going through what we’ve gone through.”

(Compiled by Graham Wray)



TV GOLD

RIZ AHMED’S performance on Amazon Prime’s brilliant comedy/drama Bait, (hat tip, Tony Parsons) which, among other things, has taught me the Urdu for crocodile dick: “Magarmach ka dic.”

Harry Redknapp’s Seann “Stuart” Walsh put-down on I’m A Celeb: South Africa.

Sky Atlantic repeating Chernobyl, one of the greatest dramas ever made, to mark the disaster’s 40th anniversary.

And KSI finally getting the point of Britain’s Got Talent by awarding Mr Cherry, a Japanese bloke who can open champagne bottles with his butt cheeks, a golden buzzer.

Who knows, the live shows may not be a total, sob story- ridden yawn now.

THE Assembly: “Greetings Sir Lenny Henry. What’s the hardest decision you had to forgive yourself for?”

Everything except Tiswas.

GREAT TV lies and delusions of the month.

I’m A Celeb: South Africa, Seann Walsh: “You can see why the nation loves Gemma Collins. She’s fantastic.”



Miriam Margolyes Made Me Me, Simon Draper: “Miriam Margolyes is everyone’s favourite person. You want her to like you.”

And Good Morning Britain, Katie Price: “I’m healthy, don’t worry about me.”

You’re not and I wasn’t.

COINCIDENCE of the week?

The Secret Sex Lives Of Tyrants, Fathali Moghaddam: “It’s been said, Fidel Castro slept with 35,000 women in communist Cuba.”

The World Snooker Championship, Stephen Hendry: “John Higgins wants to screw his way through as many reds as possible.”

So there is a precedent.

POLITICAL lesson of the week?

The Secret Sex Lives Of Tyrants: “Chairman Mao, founder of communist China, was a disgusting, filthy and contaminated person who stank, who had pus dripping from his gums, whose eyes were crusted over and God knows what he did with other secretions.”



Which just goes to show, purely based on his appearance, we shouldn’t dismiss Zack Polanski either.

Lookalike of the week

THIS week’s winner is BBC newsreader Reeta Chakrabarti and the great Melvyn Hayes, from It Ain’t Half Hot Mum.

Sent in by David Sinclair, Larbert, Falkirk.

News.title: Summer BA strike fears as pilots are balloted over ‘kamikaze’ new pay deal
News.content:
BA PAY STRIKE LOOMS Summer BA strike fears as pilots are balloted over ‘kamikaze’ new pay deal

BRITISH Airways is facing the prospect of strikes as its pilots are balloted over a “kamikaze” pay deal.

The 79-page package of proposals includes bonuses for captains to carry less fuel, sparking safety fears.



Pilots say the changes leave them worse off despite a 2.5 per cent pay rise increasing to four per cent.

The changes include reduced pension contributions and a cut in the hourly Flying Pay Supplement



The proposal also includes replacing future talks with “trust and goodwill”.

It has sparked fears of BA forcing changes.

Critics add that less than half of crew can vote on the plan, as it has been sent only to British Airline Pilots’ Association union members.

A senior flyer said: “It’s a kamikaze proposal for BA pilots.

“Even Balpa states, ‘This deal does produce uncertainty and risk for members more than any traditional pay award’.”

BA said it is “committed to making improvements to colleagues’ experience at work”.

Balpa said “members will decide” if it supports the proposal.

The ballot closes next week.

News.title: Fears ancient art of tea leaf reading is dying out as Gen Z Brits turn their backs on fortune telling
News.content:
A TEA-LEAF reader fears it is dying out as Gen Z turn their backs on fortune-telling.

Michele Liddle, 41, comes from a family of readers, with her mother, grans and two great-grans all interpreting patterns and symbols formed by loose tea leaves left in a cup.





Since going professional in 2015, Michele says she has helped predict new jobs, pregnancies and relationships.

But she said: “I fear this ancient art is dying out because no one is prepared to learn the skills.

”We used to have conversations with our grandparents and have tea and biscuits and talk about tea leaves.

”Women used to read their leaves for fun, but that doesn’t happen often at all now.

“I don’t think many people are interested in it any more which is a real shame.”

Tea-leaf reading originated in ancient China and is known as tasseography.

Michele, from Amble, Northumberland, charges £67 for an online reading and follows strict rules.

She stirs the tea three times, flips the cup and turns it clockwise three times before tapping it three times.



Loose Earl Grey is her preferred brew.

Michele learned from her mum when she was young.

She said: “When my grandad passed away in 2015 I started to get back into my spirituality.

“My grandmother taught my mum but then on my dad’s side, my other grandmother used to do tea-leaf readings.

“We used to go to seances and do other spooky stuff together.”



Michele is behind the launch of Northumberland Haunted Museum and is launching tea-leaf reading workshops.

She said it was normal to be dubious, adding: “One of my biggest sceptics is my husband.”

News.title: Starmer drama will not paralyse the country for much longer… here’s how I know it’s a matter of when, not if, he goes
News.content:
KEIR STARMER’S handling of the Peter Mandelson fiasco has been like an episode of the TV sitcom Yes, Prime Minister.

His convoluted attempts to dodge blame for the botched appointment echo the verbal jousting between senior civil servants and their political master in the hit show.





Perhaps it’s time to dust down the 1980s series for a reboot, or better still, hand the levers of power to Jim Hacker.

He might at least bring some laughter to proceedings.

You can just imagine the exchanges if the celebrated comedy actors had moved into No10 to appoint the new ambassador to Washington.

PM: “I think we can agree that appointing Peter Mandelson would strengthen transatlantic relations.”

Sir Humphrey: “Strengthen, Prime Minister?”

PM: “Yes, strengthen.

“He’s very experienced.”

Sir Humphrey: “Experience is merely history’s way of saying we have seen what happens before and have chosen to proceed regardless.”



PM: “Get to the point, Humphrey. Should we appoint Mandelson or not?”

Sir Humphrey smiles warmly. “Prime Minister, that depends entirely on whether we are speaking in the present tense, future conditional, oh my god you’re forking kidding me or the ceremonial subjunctive.”

PM stares. “What’s the ceremonial subjunctive?”

Sir Humphrey: “It’s the tense used for decisions that will be announced, celebrated, and widely reported before the results of the vetting process are known.”

PM: “And what happens if the vetting goes wrong?”



Sir Humphrey: “You deny all knowledge and issue a clarification.”

Prime Minister: “Will that help?”

Sir Humphrey: “Not particularly, Prime Minister.

“But it will create the impression that something has been clarified.”

Sir Keir wasn’t playing for laughs, however, and the appalling reality is that after days of Commons statements and scrutiny, the details are as clear as mud.



The facts are simple.

He hired a friend of a jailed paedophile with business links to Russia and China to be our ambassador to the USA.

Whatever the truth, we are now witnessing the endgame.

The scandal is the penultimate nail in the PM’s coffin and the final one could be hammered home in two weeks after the expected local elections rout.

It is becoming increasingly difficult for even the most loyal ministers to take to the airwaves and spend so much political capital defending him.



The wheels of government have ground to a halt as all the energy inside No10 is burned up defending the lame-duck PM.

It’s now a matter of when, not if, he goes.

All that is keeping Sir Keir in place now is the lack of a replacement the Labour Party can unite behind.

The two favourites — Andy Burnham and Angela Rayner — set tongues wagging about a challenge after holding secret late-night talks last week.

Neither can move yet as Manchester Mayor Mr Burnham doesn’t have a Commons seat and former Deputy PM Ms Rayner is still awaiting the outcome of an HMRC inquiry into her tax affairs.



So long as these two are the front-runners, Sir Keir is safe.

Health Secretary Wes Streeting is also a strong contender but does he have the nerve to move first?

Despair in Labour ranks will only intensify as MPs go out canvassing over the next fortnight.

Voters have seen enough already with the freebies, cronyism, U-turns galore, and bad judgment calls.



Labour activists will tell them the PM has had a good war.

But that’s only because he dithered and did nothing.

But it doesn’t wash with the general public.

Most people just want the change they were promised, when all they got was rising prices, more small boat migrants, taxes at a record high, rampant inflation and stagnant growth.

There’s little chance of him tackling those problems now as he is consumed by firefighting, with his sacked chief of staff Morgan McSweeney and Foreign Office mandarin Sir Philip Barton, who opposed Mandelson’s appointment, giving evidence to MPs next week.



The wheels of government are no longer turning.

All the energy in No10 is being spent on shoring up his position.

It’s not merely the trust of the British public he’s now lost.

He is in danger of destroying the crucial working relationship with real-life Sir Humphreys.

Sir Keir took power promising a “one-team approach” to restore respect and co-operation between ministers and civil servants.



Yet after less than two years in office, he is already on his third Cabinet Secretary and last week Sir Olly Robbins became the second permanent secretary to be fired at the Foreign Office.

Senior officials believe they are being made scapegoats for the PM’s own failings.

He’s also fired two chiefs of staff and is currently searching for his fifth director of communications.

An insider said: “He’s thrown so many people under the bus; it’s getting a bit crowded down there now.”

Former Cabinet Secretary Lord Robin Butler, 88, accused him of committing a “grave injustice” by sacking Sir Olly.



He believes it has done “a great deal of harm” to relations with the civil service and believes he should be reinstated.

It’s now clear that Sir Keir will not lead Labour into the next general election and any delay in removing him after the May 7 elections will only plunge Labour into a summer of strife.

The never-ending Starmer drama will not be allowed to paralyse the country for much longer.

But it is in the hands of his own Cabinet.

Will they have the courage to tell him what he must already know they are itching to say?



One thing is clear, when Sir Keir asks the men in grey suits if it is time to go they will answer with one voice:

Yes, Prime Minister.

LET’S BAN ALL MOBILE MENACES MOBILE phones will be banned by law in schools after yet another U-turn by the PM. Children will be forbidden from using them during lessons, moving between classrooms, at break time and lunch. This is one policy reversal that will be welcomed by most teachers and parents. But why stop there? If we’re serious about tackling irritating smartphone habits, let’s go further. Top of my hit list would be public transport. Anyone who watches videos on full volume during the morning commute should be catapulted off at the next stop. Then there’s restaurants. If you photograph your meal for longer than it takes to eat it, staff should be allowed to repossess your dessert. Even more annoying are those at the gym, who occupy an exercise bench while doom scrolling through Instagram, blissfully unaware that others are waiting to use the equipment. And don’t get me started on pavements. The slow, weaving text-walker is a menace. No-text zones should be set up in busy stations, high streets and department stores to restore traffic flow. Most hideous of all is talking on the phone while spending a penny. I wonder what the person on the other end would say if they knew? It’s downright disrespectful. Finally, family gatherings. One scroll at the dinner table, and Grandma gets to read your last three WhatsApp messages out loud. Suddenly, eye contact wouldn’t seem so bad after all.

NIGEL FARAGE says every school in England will be required to fly the flag and honour our patron saint if Reform UK wins the next election.

A good idea, but his patriotic curriculum will sadly come too late for senior Labour politicians.

London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan was forced to delete his St George’s Day message this week after he posted it on the wrong day.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Sir Keir Starmer did get the date right but didn’t mention England once in his 357-work address, referring only to Britain.

Back to school for both of them.

News.title: Brit vicar who described himself as ‘wild child’ abused multiple girls at youth group before fleeing to Australia
News.content:
PRIEST PROBE Brit vicar who described himself as ‘wild child’ abused multiple girls at youth group before fleeing to Australia

A BRIT vicar who called himself a “wild child” abused multiple girls before fleeing to Australia, according to a review.

The Rev Kesh Govan, 50, took his own life in November after allegations of sexual misconduct with girls at a youth group in the UK were found to be “substantiated”.





Following his death, the Anglican Church Southern Queensland launched an independent investigation.

The probe has now concluded that Govan had groomed and sexually abused several victims.

The investigation said it found the vicar had “groomed and sexually abused multiple female children within one youth group while living in the United Kingdom“.

Govan, who was also known as the Singing Vicar, was born a Hindu, but later converted to Christianity following a near-death experience.

Originally born in Bolton, Greater Manchester, Govan trained in Durham before becoming a vicar in Bolton.

He moved later in life to Ireland, and then to Brisbane, Australia.

While living in the UK, he worked as DJ on a local radio station and took part in school chapel services.

The new review said attendees of the church in Brisbane where Govan had served had been given “a confidential pathway for people to come forward if they, or someone they know was groomed or sexually abused by Govan”.



The report said: “The Govan family, who had no knowledge of Govan’s sexual abuse of children prior to his death, and the St Stephen’s, and All Saints communities have also been offered free confidential counselling and support.”

It reportedly found no evidence that Govan had committed any offences in Australia.

The Most Rev Jeremy Greaves, the Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane, said: “On behalf of the church, I would like to issue a sincere and complete apology to the survivors of Govan’s child sexual abuse.

“Over the past decade, the church, both in Australia and the United Kingdom, has strengthened its policies, procedures, and protocols. However, it must do better.

“The evidence detailed within the independent investigation report has been shared with authorities in Australia and the United Kingdom.”



The Dioceses of Manchester and Lichfield, where Govan previously served, said they were “deeply distressing above all for those who have experienced abuse, and also for families, friends and communities”.

Govan once described himself as a wild child in an interview with the Irish Independent in 2005.

He was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease when he turned 18.

Govan said he had been ill for three years and had been told he had the final stages of cancer.

He met some Christians and started to pray for help, before his cancerous cells were found and he made a full recovery, he said.

News.title: Moment tomato juice is thrown over exiled crown prince of Iran by protester as he calls for overthrow of Ayatollah
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment the exiled crown prince of Iran was attacked with tomato juice in Berlin.

Footage showed Reza Pahlavi being splashed by the red liquid as he left a press conference.





A man can be seen spraying the 65-year-old’s neck and jacket with the juice before being seized and detained by cops.

Moments before the attack, Pahlavi had denounced the US-Iran ceasefire.

A police spokesman said Pahlavi had been struck “in front of the building with a red liquid, apparently tomato juice”. He was not hurt.

The spokesman said an investigation was underway into alleged “bodily harm, property damage and insults against persons in political life”.



During the conference Pahlavi urged European governments not to appease Iran’s leadership.

The exiled prince warned that attempts to negotiate with the rogue state would only keep the current system in power.

“If you think you can make peace with this regime, you are sorely mistaken,” he said.

“There will never be stability, even if a watered-down version of this system survives.”



Claiming that 19 political prisoners were executed in Iran in the past two weeks, Pahlavi asked if the “free world” would continue to “watch the slaughter in silence”.

“The regime has never been as fragile as it is now,” he added.

Who is Reza Pahlavi? CROWN Prince Reza Pahlavi has pledged to end the barbaric rule of Iran’s fundamentalist firebrands – by restoring a UK-style monarchy Silver-haired Pahlavi, 65, has vowed to order elections and bow to a new democratically chosen government if he returns to his homeland after nearly five decades in exile. He believes he is the figurehead needed to oust the mullahs who have crushed dissent with brutality since 1979. He was 18 when his father, Iran’s last Shah, fled in 1979 as the Islamic Revolution replaced Iran’s corrupt monarchy. The playboy Shah, who died in Egypt in 1980, was loathed after pocketing oil revenues as his people faced poverty. Pahlavi promised to lead a revolt to free his people while seeking no power. He lives in exile in the United States and has not ruled Iran, but is a prominent opposition figure calling for a secular, democratic Iran. Pahlavi is a key symbol for anti-regime protesters, regularly speaking out against Iran’s clerical leadership and supporting recent protest movements. He said he would be “a steward of a national transition to democracy”. But he is yet to win the backing of Donald Trump who is not convinced Pahlavi has enough support.

“It is a wounded beast.”

Pahlavi is the eldest son of the former Shah of Iran – the last leader before the dynasty was overthrown in the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

He fled Iran as a teen and has been living just outside of Washington DC since 2001.



The former prince has put himself forward as a potential leader for a democratic Iran.

It comes as Iran’s top officials released what appears to be a joint statement, vowing “obedience to the Supreme Leader of the revolution”.

In a post on X president of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian: “In our Iran, there are no extremists or moderates; we are all ‘Iranians’ and ‘revolutionaries,’ and with the iron unity of the nation and the state, and with full obedience to the Supreme Leader of the Revolution, we will make the criminal aggressor regret it.

“One God, one nation, one leader, and one path; and that path to victory for Iran is dearer than life.”

It comes after US President Donald Trump extended the deadline to reach a long-term agreement on Tuesday.



A specific date for when the ceasefire will expire remains unclear.

Hopes of a deal to end the war were dashed as the rogue state inflicted “heavy damage” on one ship as the crew dived for cover.

But Trump has warned he “expects to be bombing” if a deal is not struck.

News.title: 'African tribe' leader deported after setting up camp in UK woods
News.content:
'African tribe' leader deported after setting up camp in UK woods

Kofi Offeh has been deported from the UK after branding himself the leader of 'Kingdom of Kubala', a 'lost African tribe' who set up camp in a Scottish woodland last year

View 3 Images Kofi Offeh, 36, has been deported after camping illegally in woodland last year (Image: Katielee Arrowsmith / SWNS)

A man who led a self-styled 'lost African tribe' in a Scottish woodland has been deported, the Home Office has confirmed.

‌



Kofi Offeh - who uses the name King Atehene - became locked in a fierce legal battle last year with local residents, police and the local council after setting up camp near Jedburgh in the Scottish Borders.

‌



Calling themselves the Kingdom of Kubala, the group of three - including one woman he described as his 'Queen', and the other his 'handmaiden' - claimed to be ancient inheritors of the land and descendants of 'Black Jacobites' who were promised the land 400 years ago. They refused to leave the area for around four months, and were evicted in October after a dramatic police raid.

‌



View 3 Images King Atehehe, Queen Nandi and handmaiden Asnat claimed they were the descendants of 'Black Jacobites' (Image: Katielee Arrowsmith / SWNS)

Tonight, the Home Office confirmed that Mr Offeh has been deported back to Ghana. It comes after local media showed him arriving at Kotoko international airport in the capital Accra earlier this week.

One video reported to have been taken shortly after landing showed him again identifying himself as a "King" and promising a "new wave of the Kingdom of Kubala".

‌



He told the camera: "All the police are going to serve me, all the chiefs are going to bow before me, if you have a president, he will have to kneel before me".

Mr Offeh, 36, lived at the camp in Scotland with 43-year-old wife Jean Gasho, who called herself "Queen Nandi", and a third member, 21-year-old Kaura "Asnat" Taylor, who told her social media followers she was an "inferior mistress" and a "surrogate for the queen".

View 3 Images The group were evicted after several months camping around Jedburgh, Scotland (Image: Katielee Arrowsmith / SWNS)

‌



Ms Taylor, from Dallas, Texas, was released in October after being arrested by immigration enforcement. The Scottish Borders Council originally removed the trio from a privately-owned camp on a hillside overlooking Jedburgh in July.

Instead of leaving the area entirely, the group simply relocated roughly a mile outside of town, settling into a patch of woodland next to an industrial estate.

After sheriff officers ousted them from their second makeshift camp, they moved on property belonging to the Scottish Borders Council located a few metres away.

Article continues below

The council pursued legal action through the courts to remove the 'tribe', who were ultimately evicted last October during a joint early-morning raid carried by police, sheriff officers, and immigration enforcement.

All three were seen being led away from the area, with council workers later seen tossing bags filled with blankets, clothing, and food supplies into a bin lorry.

Ms Taylor was detained by immigration officers during the raid but was later released, while Ms Gasho (Queen Nandi) left the scene separately in a pickup vehicle.

News.title: Louisiana mall mass shooting leaves multiple hurt with two critical as manhunt launched
News.content:
Louisiana mall mass shooting leaves multiple hurt with two critical as manhunt launched

Members of the public have been urged to avoid the Mall of Louisiana after a shooting near the shopping centre's food court left ten people injured

View 2 Images Armed police at the scene (Image: BCasserleigh/X)

A shooting at a shopping centre in Louisiana has left two people critically injured and multiple others hurt.

‌



The Baton Rouge Police Department says ten people were injured in connection with the incident at the Mall of Louisiana, with armed police swarming the scene and quickly placing it under lockdown. Some of the victims are undergoing surgery, police say.

‌



The shooting is believed to have happened near the shopping centre's food court at 1:25pm local time, with a triage set up by paramedics outside a JCPenney store. The drive to enter and exit the mall has been cleared for emergency responders only.

‌



According to Chief TJ Morse, there is no threat to the public at this time, and that the shooting was sparked by an argument between two groups that escalated.

View 2 Images An armed officer at the scene (Image: X)

Sid Edwards, the Mayor-president of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, said he is on scene at the mall where a command post has been set up.

‌



"There has been a shooting with multiple victims," Edwards said in a statement. "All civilians have been safely escorted out of the mall. Please keep the victims and their families in your prayers."

Joining police at the scene, he said: "To the thugs who did this, we are going to catch you."

Local Governor Jeff Landry said he is "aware of the active shooter scene at the Mall of Louisian" and urged people "please avoid the area".

‌



"Sharon and I are praying for those affected and are grateful for a quick response by our law enforcement officials," he added.

Attorney General Liz Murrill said: "I have spoken to District Attorney Hillar Moore, who is actively monitoring the situation involving a weapon or weapons being discharged in the Food Court at the Mall of Louisiana.

"Multiple law enforcement agencies are responding – please avoid the area. More details will be available soon."

News.title: Claim evil predator who encouraged Brighton beach gang-rape 'has murder conviction'
News.content:
Claim evil predator who encouraged Brighton beach gang-rape 'has murder conviction'

Karin Al-Danasurt, 20, was found guilty of four counts of rape as a secondary party by encouraging and filming the brutal attack

View 3 Images Karin Al-Danasurt was found guilty of four counts of rape as a secondary party by encouraging and filming the attack (Image: Sussex Police/PA Wire)

A vile predator who filmed a woman being raped on Brighton beach by his two twisted friends was in the UK in a bid to avoid jail after being convicted of murder in Egypt, prosecutors have said.

Karin Al-Danasurt, 20, was found guilty of four counts of rape as a secondary party by encouraging and filming the horror attack in October last year. The victim was targeted by the men as she was "staggering in the street" and "incapacitated" in the early hours of October 4 last year, Hove Crown Court heard. She said she heard laughter as she was attacked.

Al-Danasurt was convicted after a trial alongside Ibrahim Alshafe, 25, and Iranian Abdulla Ahmadi, 26, who were each found guilty of two counts of rape. The trio all arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel by boat and had decisions pending on asylum claims.

Details of Al-Danasurt's alleged past crimes emerged at a plea hearing in November last year, ahead of the trial, but the judge withdrew the evidence from the case after his defence team contested the conviction.

3 View 3 Images Karin Al-Danasurt appears to grin as he leaves Hove Crown Court (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire) 3 View 3 Images Ibrahim Alshafe, 25, Abdulla Ahmadi, 26, and Karin Al-Danasurt, 20, have been found guilty (Image: Sussex Police)

At the time, prosecutors told the court Al-Danasurt had been convicted of murder in his absence in Egypt, adding that the basis of his asylum claim was that he fled the country to "evade a lengthy custodial sentence". But his defence barrister said it was in fact his brother who had the conviction for murder, not him.

They added that the UK Government’s assessment of Egypt is that a person who is openly critical of the government is likely to be at risk of serious harm. As a result, the evidence was not heard by jurors during the trial because of the dispute.

On Thursday, prosecutor Hanna Llewellyn-Waters KC told the court there were "ongoing inquiries at a very senior level" about Al-Danasurt's crimes abroad, adding he had also been given a caution in the UK for criminal damage in April last year but said she was "not in a position" to provide any more detail.

In the wake of the verdicts, border security and asylum minister Alex Norris said: "Once sentencing has taken place, we will move to deport them off British soil."

At the time of the attack, all three defendants knew each other and were living at Home Office-approved hotel accommodation for asylum seekers in Lower Beeding near Horsham, West Sussex.

Al-Danasurt was born in Egypt and went to school there until around the age of 11, and left Egypt to come to the UK in June 2022.

UK weather maps reveal snow to hit 30 counties within days – see full list

UK weather maps suggest that up to 30 counties could be hit with snow between May 6 and May 8, as the Met Office warns of a 'more changeable and unsettled spell' ahead

View 5 Images Parts of Scotland, northern England and Wales could see snow, UK weather maps suggest (Image: PA)

UK weather maps have revealed that up to 30 counties could be hit by snow soon as the Met Office warns of a "more changeable or unsettled spell of weather".

‌



The latest maps from WXCharts, which uses data from MetDesk, suggest that between May 6 (Wednesday) and May 8 (Friday) parts of Scotland, northern England and Wales could see snow showers or a dusting of snow.

‌



The cooler, more wintry snap is expected to come after a run of largely dry conditions, with a mix of sunshine and cloud through late April and into early May, driven by high pressure, according to the Met Office.

‌



WXCharts maps shows bands of heavy rain sweeping across much of country around midday on Wednesday, May 6. But the purple shading - indicating snow - suggests large parts of Scotland, along with some areas of Northern England, particularly the Pennines, could see snow as temperatures dip.

View 5 Images The map suggests counties in Scotland and northern England could see snow at noon on May 6 (Image: WXCharts)

By the evening of May 6, the worst of the wet weather looks set to clear, with scattered showers expected in western parts of the country. However, the Grampians and Snowdonia could still see some snow by around 9pm.

‌

News.title: 'The Assisted Dying Bill cannot wait for ever - but it cannot be rushed either'
News.content:
'The Assisted Dying Bill cannot wait for ever - but it cannot be rushed either'

'The story of Wendy Duffy stops you cold and breaks your heart as she is travelling abroad to end her life because Britain has no answer for yer yet'

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

When grief is too much

Wendy Duffy picked her outfit. She chose her song. She said her goodbyes. A mother shattered by the loss of her son - a young man of 23, taken in the cruellest, most ordinary of moments - she has decided she simply cannot go on.

‌



Her story stops you cold. It breaks your heart. And it forces every one of us to ask the hardest question there is: when does compassion mean letting someone go?

‌



Here is a woman not terminally ill, but consumed by a grief so total it has swallowed her whole. She is travelling abroad to end her life because Britain has no answer for her yet.

‌



The Assisted Dying Bill is now almost certainly dead for this parliament - buried under 1,200 Lords amendments, time running out before May.

Both sides bear responsibility for that failure. But Wendy's case cuts to the very heart of why this matters. This is not just about choice. It is about vulnerability, despair and whether any law can ever truly protect the most fragile among us. This cannot wait forever. But it cannot be rushed either.

‌



Boweled over

British science is once again leading the fight to save lives.

A groundbreaking NHS trial of a new immunotherapy drug offers real hope against bowel cancer - a disease killing nearly 17,000 Britons a year and rising among the under-50s. Stories like Nick Cleworth’s are remarkable.

His tumour vanished without life-changing surgery. It is not just progress, it is transformation. This is the legacy of pioneers like Dame Deborah James, whose courage put this disease in the spotlight.

Article continues below

But early diagnosis still matters. Symptoms can be subtle and too often ignored. Britain’s scientists are delivering hope to the world. Now we must match it with awareness, investment and action to ensure more lives are saved.

Loss of Focus

The final whistle for Football Focus is a sad one. For more than half a century, it has been part of the fabric of football on Saturday. Falling audiences may explain the decision, but something valuable is lost. Not everything needs reinventing. Some traditions are worth protecting, not discarding.

News.title: Girl, 10, finds endangered Mexican axolotl under bridge in the UK
News.content:
Girl, 10, finds endangered Mexican axolotl under bridge in the UK

Evie Hill, 10, from Leciester, discovered a critically endangered nine-inch Mexican axolotl in the River Ogmore in Bridgend, Wales - and it's now living with her at home

View 3 Images Evie, 10, has named the Mexican axolotl Dippy (Image: Melanie Hill / SWNS)

An endangered Mexican axolotl has been found in Britain for the first time by an adventurous 10-year-old girl.

‌



Evie Hill, from Leicester, discovered the nine-inch Mexican axolotl after spending a day paddling with her mum Melanie in the River Ogmore in Bridgend, Wales earlier this month.

‌



It's the first time an axolotl has been found in the wild in the United Kingdom - and the type she found is endangered, with only 50 to 1,000 thought to be left anywhere in the world.

‌



The 10-year-old told how she was turning over rocks underneath a bridge when she spotted the amphibian - and recognised the species straight away from her favourite computer game, Minecraft.

View 3 Images The adventurous schoolgirl found the endangered amphibian underneath a bridge in Wales (Image: Melanie Hill / SWNS)

Missing capybara Samba still on the run after 37 days as stolen camera traps hamper search READ MORE :

She said: "I was just playing down by the river lifting things up to see what I could find and I lifted up a green mat and saw an axolotl. "I knew what it was straight away because I saw its gills. I have seen them on Youtube on Minecraft videos and other videos showing how to look after them. "I ran up to my mum shouting 'I've found an axolotl, I've found an axolotl' - but she did not believe me at all. But she told me not to go back in the water and then I went down to the bank and spotted it again. "So I jumped in and caught it with my hands. I went back to my mum and said 'I'm sorry I broke the rules but look I've caught the axolotl'. She was quite shocked."

‌



View 3 Images The axolotl now lives with Evie's family, as it is illegal to release them into the wild (Image: Melanie Hill / SWNS)

Under the the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, it is illegal to release an axolotl into the environment, as it is a non-native species - and so they made the decision to bring it home.

"We put it in a gravy jug before going to the Range to buy a tub", Evie said. "We couldn't put it back in the water as it is illegal to so we brought it back home. My friends at school think it's really cool."

‌



The Mexican axolotl is now living with Evie and Melanie at the family home in Leicester. Evie has given him the name Dippy, in honour of how he was discovered.

Chris Newman, director of the National Centre for Reptile Welfare, told the BBC Evie probably saved Dippy's life when she discovered it.

He said there were no recorded sightings of Mexican axolotls in the UK or elsewhere in the world. He added: "This is a quite a unique situation, and I think the young female has a keen eye to actually spot it.

Article continues below

"I think she did remarkable to find him. Catching them is no mean feat - they're quite slippery, so I think she did really well."

News.title: Strictly's Craig Revel Horwood thanks BBC licence fee payers for lavish life with £2m home
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Strictly's Craig Revel Horwood thanks BBC licence fee payers for lavish life with £2m home

Strictly Come Dancing judge Craig Revel Horwood has revealed the real reason he would never do US counterpart Dancing With The Stars - and you'll never guess what it is...

View 5 Images Craig Revel Horwood is the longest standing judge on Strictly (Image: PA Wire)

Outspoken Strictly judge Craig Revel Horwood has likened himself to murdered Beatle John Lennon, in an unfiltered conversation with fans. His bizarre comparison came after declaring he would not join sister show Dancing With The Stars in the US, for fear of being assassinated by a deranged fan, like the Imagine singer, who was gunned down outside his New York apartment in 1980 by Mark Chapman.

‌



Craig, 61, said: "I have never done Dancing With The Stars. No, thank God. I think I would be like Lennon and get shot. Don't you think? There are so many guns over there darling, I don’t think I’d like to.” His revelation came at the launch of the 49-date tour of his new show Revelations - Songs Boys Don't Sing at Chequer Mead Theatre in East Grinstead on Wednesday night.

‌



Claiming he was offered the Dancing With The Stars job, he added: “I was put on standby as a matter of fact, when Len [Goodman] and Bruno [Tonioli] got it. But I am sort of pleased it did not work out. You have to make a decision in life, whether that is all you want to do. They were doing two [series] a year and I have a glittering career on the stage as a director and choreographer, so I did not want to give that up. Also, my directorial career was just taking off and I did not want to ruin that, as I love doing operas and those sort of things.”"

‌



View 5 Images John Lennon was gunned down outside his New York apartment in 1980 by Mark Chapman. (Image: Getty Images)

No stranger to controversy, at the Wednesday night gig, he told 330 fans he had the BBC licence fee payers to thank for his lavish lifestyle. Owner of a £2m mansion in leafy King's Cliffe, Northamptonshire, which he bought in 2021, Craig - who earns £200K a year from Strictly - said: "If I am ‘nice’ I won’t make any money, darling. But it has worked out rather well. I have got an eight bedroom mansion with a swimming pool. My dressing box at home is one room … thanks to all your wonderful TV licences.

"No, I have been very fortunate. I mean, Strictly has been brilliant as a Saturday job, but it did cast me as the villain, I suppose. But I love playing the villain in panto, as they always get the best numbers to sing. They get the best writing, best costumes and generally the villain is only on for 15 minutes of the show and you get paid a fortune."

‌



Craig also moaned that the cost of renovating his eight bedroom home had meant postponing plans to marry fiancé Jonathan Myring, 39. The pair have been together since 2018, after Strictly super-fan Myring met Craig backstage on the Strictly Come Dancing live tour in Nottingham.

Last year, Craig got the green light to build a luxury party terrace, complete with a spa and hot tub at his riverside mansion - despite opposition from neighbours, fearful of increased noise. He has also won permission for a large entrance hall, gym, master bedroom, butler's kitchen, wine store and snug.

View 5 Images Strictly judges Craig, Shirley, Motsi and Anton (Image: CREDIT LINE:BBC/Kieron McCarron)

‌



Craig continued: "We are still not married. We have been engaged for years and years and years. Something keeps stopping our wedding. I don’t know why. I think it might be to do with money as I am doing a renno [renovation]." When they do tie-the-knot, he hopes to enlist his friend, Aussie cabaret artist Alison Jiear, to conduct the ceremony, adding: "We will get married soon. We will do it when the house is finished. It could be 2027."

One person who is unlikely to be invited is Spitting Image and Dead Ringers voiceover star, Jan Ravens, who was booted off during the early rounds of Strictly in 2006, when her jive with Anton du Beke failed to impress. Her husband, Universal Music vice president Max Hole, allegedly confronted Craig in the BBC bar after her elimination. Craig said: "Jan Ravens thought it was my fault that she went out. She came up to me when she got ousted. It was the audience that voted her out, not me thank you very much.

"She came up to me and said ‘this is all your fault’. And then her husband bashed me up at the BBC bar that night. Yeah I know. I went to the press the next day and it got me a lot of coverage darling." Craig was more positive towards other Strictly stars,

‌



He said: "Who are my favourite three celebs that have done Strictly? I am going to say the cricketer Mark Ramprakash. He was really bad until a Saturday. On a Friday in rehearsals he was a shocker. He did not remember anything, but on a Saturday night it must have been like being in a stadium. He switched on and was fantastic. I also liked Anne Widdecombe when she was dressed like Big Bird and she had to wear tights to protect her modesty. I also loved Alesha Dixon and Rose [Ayling-Ellis] and Giovanni [Pernice]. They were just gorgeous."

5 View 5 Images Craig Revel Horwood and boyfriend Jonathan Myring pictured at home in Hampshire. (Image: Sunday Mirror) 5 View 5 Images Craig Revel Horwood as The Wicked Stepmother pictured outside The Theatre Royal in Nottingham city centre (Image: Joseph Raynor/ Reach PLC)

‌



Keenly awaiting the return of Strictly in September, complete with new presenters, for now Australian Craig is looking forward to touring his one man show until the end of June. He said: "I have just come back from Australia. I have been there for six weeks. I am so jet lagged. I am happy to say I will be returning to Dancing with the Stars in Australia next year too. They did not do it this year because of the Olympics or the Commonwealth Games or something.

"But I have been doing it for the last three years and we are doing it again next year. It allows me to see my family. My mum is 84 and she is still kicking on and going strong. She has had two bouts of cancer and won her battle. I am also working on a new musical, called NOW That's What I Call A Musical. We did one about the 80s’ music but we are now doing one about the 90s.

"I always thought I would like to do Gypsy but ever since Imelda Staunton did it in the West End I don’t know whether I could do a better job. It has sort of been done. I love the story about a desperate woman wanting to be the star and she lost her life and gave it to her daughter, forcing her daughter into prostitution. It is right up my alley."

News.title: Football Focus to end after 52 years
News.content:
Football Focus is to end after 52 years, BBC Sport has announced.

Launched in 1974, the Saturday lunchtime television programme provided fans with interviews, analysis and stories from across the game before the weekend's fixtures.

Changing audience habits have meant a growth in the use of digital platforms and on-demand to get the same pre-match content.

As a result, linear television viewing figures have gradually declined since 2018.

Football Focus will run until the end of the season.

Alex Kay-Jelski - director of BBC Sport - said: "Football Focus has been a hugely important programme in the history of BBC Sport and has played a key role in telling the stories of the game for generations of viewers.

"This decision was made before last week's wider BBC savings announcement, reflecting the continued shift in how audiences engage with football and our commitment to evolving how we deliver content to reach fans wherever they are."

From next season, Kelly Somers' The Football Interview will move to Saturday at 12:45 BST on BBC One. Final Score with Jason Mohammad will start on BBC One earlier than it has this season - at 15:45 BST.

Arsenal winger Bukayo Saka, former Chelsea manager Emma Hayes, Manchester City midfielder Bernardo Silva, Liverpool striker Hugo Ekitike and Manchester United boss Michael Carrick are among the players and coaches to have featured on The Football Interview this season.

BBC Sport says it will expand its digital output across BBC platforms, including exclusive shows on YouTube. The intention is to deliver more high-quality, accessible and engaging football coverage at scale.

Football Focus started out as part of Grandstand, with Sam Leitch presenting a pre-cursor called Football Preview.

It was renamed Football Focus, with Bob Wilson becoming an iconic figure. After first taking on presenting duties in 1974, the former Arsenal goalkeeper stayed in the role for 20 years.

Steve Rider, Gary Lineker, Ray Stubbs, Manish Bhasin and Dan Walker - for 12 years - all had stints in the chair.

Its final host will be Alex Scott, who has presented Football Focus for the past five years and will continue to work for the BBC.

"Alex Scott is one of our finest presenters, is hugely popular across the men's and women's game and is a big part of our present and future," added Kay-Jelski.

"She will remain at the heart of our sports output across both the men's World Cup this year and the Women's World Cup in 2027, as well as continuing her leadâ¯role on the Women's Super League and BBC Sports Personality of the Year.

"We are also working on a very exciting new project with her - more to come on that soon."

Scott said being part of the programme had been "incredibly special" and it was an "honour" to have been presenter for five years.

"It has been such an important part of my life, working with some of the very best people in the business, both on screen and behind the scenes," she said on Instagram.

News.title: Adam Hall’s victim speaks out as rapist jailed for deliberate HIV infections
News.content:
A victim of Adam Hall has spoken out after the 43-year-old was jailed at Newcastle Crown Court for life with a minimum term of 23 years for deliberately infecting sexual partners with HIV and raping some of his victims.

The victim in this clip, whose voice has been replaced by an actor's, was just 15 when he was infected with HIV. He found out he had contracted HIV in a phone call from health professionals moments after he stepped off a school bus.

Hall, of Washington, Tyne and Wear, hid his HIV status from partners, failed to take medication to keep his viral load low, then had unprotected sex with men, sometimes raping them.

He was convicted of five counts of rape and seven counts of causing grievous bodily harm – by deliberately infecting younger partners with HIV after meeting them in bars in the Newcastle area or on the dating app Grindr.

News.content:

Washington is buzzing with the possibility that President Donald Trump might name one or more Supreme Court justices before the November midterm elections.

In a conversation with Fox Business TV host Maria Bartiromo on April 15, 2026, Trump discussed the potential retirement of Justice Samuel Alito, 76, the reliably conservative justice appointed by President George W. Bush in 2005.

Trump praised Alito as “a great justice” and said that he is prepared to appoint a replacement, should Alito retire.

Trump added, “In theory, it’s two – you just read the statistics – it could be two, could be three, could be one.”

Trump didn’t say who the other potential retiring justices are. Speculation from pundits is that he is referring to Justice Clarence Thomas, 77, another solid conservative vote. Thomas, appointed by George H.W. Bush in 1991, is the court’s oldest justice and longest-serving member.

open image in gallery Alito raises his right hand as he participates in a ceremonial swearing-in in the East Room of the White House in Washington in February 2006 ( AFP via Getty Images )

In the same Fox interview, Trump pointed to former Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who was under intense pressure to retire during President Barack Obama’s presidency. Ginsburg opted to stay on the bench and died in September 2020.

Republicans blocked Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016 after the death of Justice Antonin Scalia. Then, in 2020, Trump replaced Ginsburg with Justice Amy Coney Barrett, solidifying a 6-3 conservative majority.

As a scholar of the Supreme Court confirmation process, I know the timing of Trump’s comments is closely linked to November’s midterm elections.

If Democrats were to take over the Senate following the midterms, it is very unlikely they would confirm a Trump-appointed Supreme Court nominee. Instead, they would probably follow the precedent set by Republicans in 2020 and block a Trump pick.

The clock is ticking on November’s midterm elections, and Democrats’ chances of taking back the Senate are improving. Assuming a current Supreme Court justice retires, here’s what has to happen for Trump and Senate Republicans to successfully confirm a successor.

The Supreme Court confirmation process

The Constitution says that the Senate provides “advice and consent” on presidential appointments to the Supreme Court. Over the course of the nation’s history, this has developed into a complex process.

Once the Senate receives a nomination from the president, it goes to the Judiciary Committee.

This is where the most public part of the confirmation process takes place: confirmation hearings. These typically last three to four days and feature a high stakes question-and-answer session with the nominee.

Prior to the hearings, senators and the nominee engage in a substantial amount of preparation.

Senators, with their staffs, do extensive background research on the nominee, which helps inform their questioning. Some of this is accomplished through the Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaire, to which nominees provide written answers. Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson’s 2022 questionnaire was 149 pages long. It included questions about organizational memberships, public speeches and judicial opinions authored.

Meanwhile, the nominee makes courtesy calls to senators to build support for confirmation.

About the author Paul M. Collins Jr. is a Professor of Legal Studies and Political Science at UMass Amherst. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

At roughly the same time, the nominee takes part in hearing preparation, known as “murder boards.” Here, the nominee’s allies play the roles of members of the Judiciary Committee, anticipating the type of tough questions the nominee will face from skeptical senators from the opposition party of the appointing president.

During Jackson’s murder boards, for instance, the focus was on expected Republican attacks that Jackson was soft on crime.

Within a few days of the end of the confirmation hearings, the Judiciary Committee votes on its recommendation to the full Senate. Then the nomination goes back to the full Senate for more discussion and a final confirmation vote. A simple majority is needed to confirm a Supreme Court nominee.

For the nine members of the court, it has taken an average of 70 days between presidential appointment and Senate confirmation, according to data from The U.S. Supreme Court Database. But this number has decreased recently, with Barrett and Jackson taking 30 and 41 days, respectively, to be confirmed.

So, as long as there is roughly a month before the November midterms, it is likely that there is enough time for the Republican Senate to confirm a Trump nominee.

Democrats have limited options

In 2017, Senate Republicans ended the filibuster for Supreme Court nominees. It was a move to secure the confirmation of Neil Gorsuch.

This reduced the threshold for confirmation from 60 votes to 51 votes. Perhaps most importantly, it also severely limited the options available to the minority party to block a Supreme Court confirmation.

open image in gallery The Constitution says that the Senate provides ‘advice and consent’ on presidential appointments to the Supreme Court ( Getty Images )

With a 53-47 Republican majority in the Senate, so long as Republicans stick together, it will be very difficult for Senate Democrats to block a Trump nominee.

There are some delay tactics available to Democrats – they can perhaps even grind the entire Senate to a halt – but they may pay a political price for these tactics. Republicans, for instance, may try to paint Democrats as obstructionist, potentially motivating a voter backlash against the Democratic Party in the midterm elections.

Nonetheless, Democrats may view this as a fight worth having, since the confirmation of another Republican-appointed justice will ensure conservative dominance on the court for decades – if not generations – to come.

News.title: Patriots coach Mike Vrabel breaks silence on Dianna Russini photo controversy
News.content:
New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel has admitted to having ‘difficult conversations’ with his family following the publication of photos of Vrabel and NFL reporter Dianna Russini.

Images of the pair holding hands at a resort in Sedona, Arizona were published by the New York Post earlier this month, reportedly taken prior to the NFL annual league meeting on March 29.

Speaking at a press conference, Vrabel said: “I’ve had some difficult conversations with people that I care about. With my family, the organisation, the coaches, the players.”

Russini stepped down from her role at The Athletic following the release of the photos, which prompted an internal review.

Since Vrabel’s statement on Tuesday (21 April), further photos of he and Russini, who are both married to other people, have surfaced.

Three professors at Atlanta's Emory University filed a lawsuit Thursday over their arrests during a 2024 campus protest over the Israel-Hamas war, saying the university broke its own free speech policies when it called in police and state troopers to aggressively disband the protest, making 28 arrests.

“The judicial system would find that Emory failed to protect its students, to protect its staff, to protect the educational mission of the university,” said philosophy Professor Noelle McAfee, one of the plaintiffs. “So this isn’t just about people’s individual rights. It’s our educational mission to train people in free and critical inquiry, to be able to learn how to engage with others, to be fearless.”

Laura Diamond, a spokesperson for Emory, said the university believes “this lawsuit is without merit.”

“Emory acts appropriately and responsibly to keep our community safe from threats of harm,” Diamond said in a statement. “We regret this issue is being litigated but we have confidence in the legal process.”

The suit is just one example of how the nationwide wave of protests continues to reverberate on elite campuses. There are many examples of lawsuits against universities by students and faculty who say they were discriminated against because of the protests. But the Emory suit is unusual. McAfee, English and indigenous studies Professor Emilio Del Valle-Escalante and economics Professor Caroline Fohlin all remain tenured faculty members and none were convicted of any charges.

The civil lawsuit in DeKalb County State Court demands that the private university repay money the three spent defending themselves against misdemeanor charges that were later dismissed, along with punitive damages. McAfee said she's suing her employer “to try to get them to be accountable and to change.”

All three say they were observers on April 25, 2024, when some students and others set up tents on the university's main quad to protest the war. They say Emory broke its own policies by calling in Atlanta police and Georgia state troopers without seeking alternatives.

McAfee was charged with disorderly conduct after she said she yelled “Stop!” at an officer roughly arresting a protester. Del Valle-Escalante said he was trying to help an older woman when he was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct. Fohlin said that when she protested against officers pinning a protester to the ground, she herself was thrown face-first to the ground and arrested, suffering a concussion and a spine injury. Fohlin was charged with misdemeanor battery of an officer.

Emory claimed that day that those arrested were outsiders who trespassed on school property. But 20 of the 28 people arrested were affiliated with the university. The professors said that after their arrests, they were targeted by threats and harassment, part of a pushback by conservatives who said universities were failing to protect Jewish students from antisemitism and allowing lawlessness.

Nationwide, advocates say there is a “Palestine exception” in which universities are willing to curb pro-Palestinian speech and protest. Palestine Legal, a legal aid group supporting such speech, said Tuesday that it received 300% more legal requests in 2025 than its annual average before 2023, mostly from college students and faculty.

McAfee served as president of the Emory University Senate after her arrest. The body makes policy recommendations and had helped draft the university’s open expression policy. She said she asked then-President Gregory Fenves in fall 2024 why Emory police weren’t dropping the charges against her and others. McAfee said Fenves told her that he wanted “to see justice.” The open expression policy was revised after 2024 to clearly prohibit tents, camping, occupations of university buildings and demonstrations between midnight and 7 a.m.

Whatever the policy, McAfee said, students are afraid to protest at Emory, saying the university has turned its back on what Atlanta Civil Rights icon John Lewis called “good trouble.”

“Students know right now that any trouble is not going to be good trouble at Emory, that they could get arrested," she said. ”So students are afraid."

In a world where third-party delivery apps such as DoorDash and Uber Eats dominate restaurant to-go orders, most pizza places still carry on the tradition of using in-house drivers.

Why spurn the convenience of a third-party to hire in-house drivers? That’s a question that industry publication Restaurant Dive answered in a recent article about the staying power of pizza delivery drivers.

Turns out the secret sauce behind in-store delivery comes in four slices: fewer added costs and headaches, better customer service, higher food quality and faster delivery times.

Businesses that hire a third-party delivery service shoulder the new costs. That means restaurants are paying extra to be on DoorDash’s network, for example. Staying with their own drivers helps pizza shops and restaurants avoid those costs and platform headaches, Eruomonitor International Research Analyst Benji Bahenma told the Restaurant Dive.

And the two other benefits? Better customer service and food quality. Pizza chains that weren’t observed using a third-party delivery service earned better food and customer service scores than those that did, a January 2026 study from customer experience consultancy Intouch Insight found.

open image in gallery Pizzerias get specific benefits from using in-house drivers that third-party delivery services haven’t quite achieved. That means the traditional pizza driver likely isn’t going away for a while ( PA Media )

Warm pizza is the key to food satisfaction, the study noted. Pizzerias that were frequently observed using third-party delivery received food temperature scores that were 14 percentage points lower than stores that didn’t use third-party delivery.

The trend continued into overall satisfaction. Companies that were never observed using a third-party delivery service scored 10 percentage points higher than pizzerias that frequently used them.

Third parties also impacted delivery times. The study found that pizzerias using in-house drivers had an average delivery time of around 30 minutes, while companies that frequently used third parties took an average of around 38 minutes.

As for companies that rarely or don’t use third-party drivers, Domino’s led the way with a 96.6 percent in-house rate, followed by Papa John’s (82.2 percent), Hungry Howie’s (75 percent), Jet’s Pizza (71.5 percent) and Marco’s Pizza (69 percent), the study noted.

MOD Pizza, Blaze Pizza and Little Caesars all used third-party drivers more than their in-house drivers.

Medium-sized pizza operators had the most to gain from improving their delivery service, Intouch noted.

open image in gallery Studies have found that third-party delivery services tend to have longer delivery times and worse customer service, than store specific drivers ( AFP/Getty )

“For mid-sized operators, this year’s results point to the continued importance of protecting food quality and managing the delivery handoff,” the report concluded. “Temperature and taste had the strongest impact on satisfaction, and the data shows how easily these can drop when insulation or delivery routines falter.”

Whether large, medium or small, it’s important that pizza brands find ways to be efficient while protecting what makes the brand great, Bahenma told Restaurant Dive.

Third-party delivery should be a “tool in the toolbox” that pizzerias use, but that companies continue to invest in their own operations and employees to ensure they provide “the best experience” and build “long-term customer relationships,” he said.

News.content:

A woman in North Carolina is facing first-degree murder charges for allegedly beating her 93-year-old husband to death with a vase.

Yorleni Shoff, 58, allegedly beat her husband, Richard, with a vase at their home in Salisbury, North Carolina around 2 am on April 9, according to the Charlotte Observer.

“The Rowan County Sheriff’s Office responded to a residence on Meadow Lane in Salisbury after 58-year-old Yorleni Shoff called 911 to report that her husband, 93-year-old Richard Shoff, was lying on the floor bleeding,” the sheriff's office said in a statement.

When deputies arrived, they found Richard Shoff on the floor of his home, unresponsive. The sheriff's statement says deputies found a "significant amount of blood indicating an assault had occurred."

Yorleni Shoff was initially arrested for assault with a deadly weapon. Her husband spent nine days in the hospital before dying from his injuries. Her charges were then upgraded to first-degree murder.

open image in gallery Yorleni Shoff, 58, is facing a first-degree murder charge after she allegedly bear her 93-year-old husband to death with a vase in their Salisbury, North Carolina home ( Rowan County Sheriff's Office )

Deputies found Yorleni Shoff at a Salisbury hotel and arrested her without incident on April 21.

“Detectives obtained a search warrant for the residence and recovered a broken vase believed to have been used as the weapon in the assault,” the sheriff’s office said. “Based on the evidence collected and the findings of the investigation, his death is being investigated as a homicide because of the injuries sustained during the assault.”

Yorlenia Shoff is being held without bond at the Rowan County Detention Center.

Her first court appearance for the murder charge is scheduled for April 22.

The investigation remains active. Anyone with information is asked to call Lieutenant Ryan Barkley (704-216-8711) or Sergant Kevin Holshouser (704-216-8683) of the Rowan County Sheriff's Office.
