World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Watchdog to audit US Department of Justice over Epstein files
World.content:
An internal US government watchdog says it will audit the justice department's handling of the Epstein files following months of controversy over redactions, missed deadlines and the publication of survivors' details.

The audit will examine how the Department of Justice (DOJ) complied with the law that forced the release of government files about late sex predator Jeffrey Epstein.

"Our preliminary objective is to evaluate the DOJ's processes for identifying, redacting, and releasing records in its possession as required by the Act," the DOJ's Office of the Inspector General (OIG) said in a statement.

The OIG theoretically operates completely independently of the department.

It could face political pressure from US President Donald Trump, who has said the country should move on from the scandal — though First Lady Melania Trump more recently gave an extraordinary statement calling for new hearings and denying rumours of involvement.

Many of the files were heavily redacted before being released by the Department of Justice. (AP Photo: Jon Elswick)

Inspector General Michael Horowitz left the watchdog last June after 13 years in the role.

He has not been replaced. The role is being filled by Deputy Inspector General William Blier, who has worked in the office since 2007.

The DOJ released millions of files in multiple tranches late last year and early this year. Many were redacted, but some survivors' details, and even naked photographs, were released.

If you or anyone you know needs help: 1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732

Men's Referral Service: 1300 766 491

Lifeline (24-hour crisis line): 13 11 14

Full Stop Australia: 1800 385 578

Bravehearts: counselling and support for survivors of child sexual abuse: 1800 272 831

Some survivors said they were "named, scrutinised, and retraumatised while Epstein's enablers continue to benefit from secrecy".

Many vowed to keep campaigning for the release of information they say is missing. In February, family of victim Virginia Roberts Giuffre told the ABC they felt the Trump administration "has basically been gaslighting us the entire time".

Loading...

The files illuminated relationships between Epstein and prominent business leaders, politicians and celebrities. A string of resignations and apologies followed.

Correspondence between Epstein and Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor prompted the brief arrest of the former prince in February.

The UK's ambassador to the US, Peter Mandelson, resigned over revelations about his relationship with Epstein. He was also later arrested, leading to a scandal that has jeopardised UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer's position.

UK braces for prospect of sixth PM in seven years Sir Keir Starmer, who led Labour to a landslide general election victory in July 2024, has become so unpopular, even some colleagues are framing his demise as a case of not if, but when.

Both Lord Mandelson and Mr Mountbatten-Windsor remain under police investigation for possible misconduct in public office, but no charges have been laid and both deny wrongdoing.

In the US, the political fallout has been less severe, though a congressional committee has been subpoenaing political figures for questioning.

Pam Bondi, who oversaw the release of the files as attorney-general, was sacked by Mr Trump earlier this month. Her handling of the issue was viewed as a likely factor, but she had also frustrated Mr Trump by not prosecuting his political adversaries more quickly.

Ms Bondi has previously argued the DOJ did its "very best" to redact and release the files in a tight timeframe and achieved a "very low" error rate. The Epstein Files Transparency Act gave 30 days for the files to be released, and allowed for redactions in certain circumstances, including for survivors' privacy.

World.title: What time is the dawn service? A guide to Anzac Day in NSW
World.content:
Thousands of people are expected to pay tribute to Australia's veteran community at Anzac Day ceremonies and events across New South Wales this long weekend.

The state will have an extra public holiday to account for April 25 falling on a weekend this year.

Here is a guide to what is happening across NSW this Anzac Day long weekend.

What time and where is Sydney's dawn service and march?

The official NSW Anzac Day Dawn Service is being held at the Cenotaph at Martin Place in Sydney from 4:20am to 5:20am on Saturday, April 25.

There will be limited seating, with standing room available when capacity is reached.

Proceedings will include the bugle call of the Last Post and a reading of the Ode of Remembrance.

A number of services are being held to commemorate Anzac Day across the state. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

The service will be followed by a march along Elizabeth Street in the CBD at 9am, with the walk to finish at Liverpool Street about 12.30pm.

A service at the Pool of Remembrance at the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park South will be held at 12:30pm.

Commemorations will return to Martin Place at 5pm for a sunset service at the Cenotaph.

Additional services are being held across the state, with location details available through RSL NSW.

How to get to the official NSW Anzac Day Dawn Service

Road closures and parking restrictions will be in place in the CBD from 1am and continuing for much of Saturday, with Transport for NSW recommending taking public transport to Anzac Day events.

Uniformed or medal-wearing members of the defence force ride public transport for free on Anzac Day. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

Travel on public transport will be free for veterans and their families on Saturday, with current or former members of the Australian Defence Force asked to wear their uniform, display service medals or carry an accreditation letter on the day.

There will be additional early-morning transport services to support dawn service access.

When is the Anzac Day public holiday for NSW?

NSW residents will have two public holidays for Anzac Day, one on Saturday and another on Monday, April 27.

Premier Chris Minns announced the additional public holiday earlier this year as part of a two-year trial.

He said no Anzac Day services would be affected by the change, but gambling game two-up will remain illegal on any other day except April 25 and Remembrance Day on November 11.

What shops will be open on Anzac Day?

In NSW, many shops and businesses are required to shut on Anzac Day, with large retailers like department stores, supermarkets and fashion outlets among those affected by the restrictions.

Trading restrictions apply to many businesses in NSW on Anzac Day. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Businesses that are exempt and will be allowed to operate on Anzac Day include:

Chemists

News agencies

Petrol stations

Cafes

Takeaway food outlets

Fruit and vegetable stores

Seafood stores

Nurseries

Licensed venues

The trading restrictions that apply to Saturday will not apply to the additional public holiday on Monday.

Full Anzac Day coverage on ABC

The ABC will provide ongoing Anzac Day coverage throughout Saturday for those who cannot attend services in person.

The Sydney dawn service will be broadcast live on ABC TV, ABC NEWS channel, ABC iview and on the ABC listen app from 4.20am (AEST), followed by the Canberra dawn service at 5.30am (AEST).

The Sydney march will be broadcast on ABC TV and ABC iview from 9am.

World.title: Service times and what's open: Your guide to Anzac Day in Queensland
World.content:
More than 500 events will be held across Queensland to commemorate Anzac Day on Saturday, April 25.

As is tradition, games of two-up will be allowed at some venues and specific trading laws will apply. The day will also be classified as a public holiday, which means many businesses will be closed or have reduced operating hours.

This is what you need to know.

Will there be a public holiday in Queensland on Monday?

No. Queensland will observe Anzac Day on Saturday and will not have an additional public holiday.

This will also be the case in the Northern Territory, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria.

In Queensland, only Industrial Relations Minister Jarrod Bleijie can substitute another day for a public holiday, according to the Queensland Holidays Act 1983.

Queensland, Northern Territory, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria will not observe an additional public holiday for Anzac Day. (ABC News: Eleni Curry)

But in January, Mr Bleijie said he would not be moving to substitute Anzac Day for another day as it fell on a Saturday.

"My understanding under the legislation is the Anzac Day falling on a Saturday is the public holiday," he said.

In New South Wales, Western Australia and the Australian Capital Territory an additional public holiday for Anzac Day will be held on Monday, April 27.

What will be open on Anzac Day?

Specific trading rules apply for licensed venues, RSL clubs and shops on Anzac Day.

Independent grocery shops, and those that predominantly sell food, can trade without restriction on Anzac Day. This also applies to cafes and essential services, and a range of exempt shops as defined by the Trading (Allowable Hours) Act 1990.

Other independent retail stores must remain closed until 1pm, and major grocery chains will be closed in Queensland.

Businesses that do open will have to pay staff penalty rates on Anzac Day due to the public holiday, and some may opt to remain closed for the day.

Dreamworld will be closed on Anzac Day. (ABC Gold Coast: Charmayne Allison)

Cinemas, amusement parks and sporting events are not permitted to open until 1:30pm, unless written permission from the industrial relations minister has been granted. Some major theme parks, including Dreamworld and Movie World, will be closed on Anzac Day.

Queensland government trading laws also prohibit real estate agents from selling property on Anzac Day, meaning alternative arrangements will have to be made for open houses and auctions.

Agents are also restricted from making phone calls, sending emails, and other activities related to the "business of selling real estate".

Flag advertising an open house inspection at a unit for sale in Brisbane. (ABC News: Kate Ainsworth)

In Queensland, RSLs and services clubs can sell and supply alcohol in association with dawn services from 5am on Anzac Day.

At other licensed venues, a meal must be served in order to sell or supply alcohol between 10am and 1pm on Anzac Day.

Business Queensland states a meal is defined as food that can be eaten with cutlery while seated, and not light takeaway food.

Patrons can buy alcohol from one hour before eating their meal and up to one hour after finishing their meal.

Ordinary trading will resume after 1pm on Anzac Day.

Can you play two-up on Anzac Day?

Yes. Two-up can be played legally in Queensland in a licensed RSL or services club on Anzac Day.

Diggers denied two-up on Anzac Day Diggers want legislation changed that allows an RSL branch to reject its application to play two-up on Anzac Day.

Written permission from an RSL sub-branch is required for two-up to be allowed in a licensed premises that is not an RSL or services club, or a services club that does not hold a liquor licence.

All money wagered in the two-up game must be returned to players as winnings, according to Business Queensland. If an entrance fee applies, any money raised must be donated to the RSL or its sub-branch.

Major Anzac Day services in Queensland

The dawn service at Brisbane's Shrine of Remembrance at Anzac Square in the CBD will start at 4:28 am. The Anzac Day Commemoration Committee recommends attendees arrive at about 3:30am.

Road closures will be in place from 3:30am to 7:30am on Ann Street, Edward Street, Adelaide Street and Creek Street.

The annual parade through Brisbane's CBD will commence at 9:45am. It will be held on Adelaide Street, between George Street and Creek Street, with road closures in place throughout the CBD until 3pm.

The Anzac Day march through the streets of Brisbane. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

In Townsville, Australia's largest garrison city, dawn services and parades will be held at two locations.

There will be dawn services at both Anzac Memorial Park and the Thuringowa Cenotaph at 5:20am.

The parade along The Strand to Anzac Memorial Park will begin at 9am.

The parade from Weir State School to Thuringowa Cenotaph will also start at 9am, followed by a service at the cenotaph at 9:30am.

Australia's largest garrison city, Townsville, will mark Anzac Day with a number of services. (ABC News: Siobhan Heanue)

A number of services will be held on the Gold Coast, including a march and dawn service on Currumbin Beach. The march will set off at 4:35am and the dawn service will start at Elephant Rock at 5am.

In Cairns, the dawn service at the cenotaph will be held at 5:30am. The march will commence at 7:30am from Fogarty Park and head up the Esplanade.

A number of services will be held on the Sunshine Coast, including a dawn service on Mooloolaba Beach at 4:55am.

ANZAC Day service at Elephant Rock on the Gold Coast. (ABC News: Steve Keen)

In Toowoomba, a dawn service will be held at Mothers' Memorial at 5am.

The march to Mothers' Memorial from the corner of Neil Street and Margaret Street will start at 10am, followed by a ceremony at 10:15am.

RSL Queensland State President Major General Stephen Day said Anzac Day was a chance for Australians to ensure the service and sacrifices of veterans are never forgotten.

"Every person who shows up, in their own way, helps to carry the spirit and living tradition forward," he said.

"It's the unity we hold when we gather in their name, to honour their service and sacrifice."

To find your local service, visit the RSL Queensland website.

World.title: The legacy of once-banned soldiers that hides in plain sight
World.content:
As a child in India, Nehchal Singh remembers playing with old war medals at his grandmother's house.

But it was not until he moved to Melbourne decades later that he discovered their origin.

Historical military documents relating to Desanda Singh's enlistment. ( )

He says he was initially in disbelief.

"I had goosebumps when I first found out," Nehchal said.

The medals were awarded to his great-grandfather, Private Desanda Singh, for his service with the Australian Imperial Force during World War I.

"There was a whole large contingent of Indian soldiers who worked alongside the British troops, but they were part of the Indian contingent," Nehchal explains.

"My great-grandfather was an ANZAC, so he was part of the Australian force."

Private Singh joined the 3rd Light Horse Regiment towards the end of the war, when rules prohibiting Australians "not substantially of European background" from enlisting were being relaxed.

He was old for a soldier, aged 38, and working as a trader with a horse and cart in the South Australian town of Ceduna.

Nehchal Singh says his great-grandfather's service gives him an "immense sense of pride". ( )

Nehchal Singh says his ancestor had a successful business, owned a farm and was well-respected in the community.

"He didn't have a need to (go to) war; he could have potentially died," Nechal says.

"There weren't a lot of people who looked like him in Australia.

" For him to be able to go and serve alongside his countrymen for his adopted country … that gives me an immense sense of pride and determination, and inspiration. "

Nehchal Singh holds the medals his grandfather, Private Desanda Singh, was awarded for his service during WWI. ( )

UNSW historian Peter Stanley said it was believed up to 20 Australians of Indian heritage served with the Anzacs, although none were on Gallipoli.

"There were about 15,000 Indians (serving with the Indian army) on Gallipoli," Professor Stanley explained. "But no Australian Indians because they weren't allowed to enlist at that point."

"It should have been impossible for Indians to serve in the Australian Imperial Force in the Great War, because the 1903 Defence Act explicitly forbade people of non-European background."

But Professor Stanley said the need for volunteers rose as the war went on and casualties mounted, allowing officers to enlist about a thousand Indigenous soldiers as well as Muslims, Sikhs and Hindus.

"Certainly there's eight men named Singh, which is the Sikh name."

An Indian driver guides his mules and artillery transport cart up a slope near Anzac Cove in 1915. ( ) An Indian driver guides his mules and artillery transport cart up a slope near Anzac Cove in 1915. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial) Troops of an Indian Army unit in their bivouac in the hills of the Gallipoli Peninsula in 1915. ( ) Troops of an Indian Army unit in their bivouac in the hills of the Gallipoli Peninsula in 1915. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial) A mounted trooper of the Indian Mysore Lancers on the Gallipoli Peninsula during WWI. ( ) A mounted trooper of the Indian Mysore Lancers on the Gallipoli Peninsula during WWI. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial) The landing beach at Anzac Cove, Gallipoli, with Indian Army soldiers in the foreground in 1915. ( ) The landing beach at Anzac Cove, Gallipoli, with Indian Army soldiers in the foreground in 1915. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

The legacy of the puggaree

Harji Singh from the Australian Sikh History Association said growing up in Australia, he found people considered the turban he wears as something relatively recent.

But he said Indians left their legacy on the Australian military a long time ago.

"Every Australian soldier that marches on Anzac Day actually wears a turban," he said.

"The 'pagri', as I say it in our language, stands for turban.

"And the 'puggaree', as Australians call it, as listed on the Australian Army website, is a seven-pleated band that goes around the slouch hat."

Harjit Singh says every Australian soldier that marches on ANZAC Day wears what could be described as a turban. ( )

The puggaree was a traditional Indian head-wrap, adopted by British soldiers in hot climates and then adapted to Australia's uniforms. The puggaree worn on Australia's slouch hat has seven pleats, one for each state and one for the Australian territories.

Professor Stanley said the pagri was also worn by other nationalities.

"All the Gurkha regiments in the Great War, including the five Gurkha battalions on Gallipoli, they also wore slouch hats, and they had puggarees too," he said.

Sikhs take pride in serving others through the military

Sikh soldiers are now a common sight in the Australian military.

They range from army reservists to senior officers.

Flight Lieutenant Kuljit Jassal says there were no other Sikhs when she joined the airforce. ( )

When Perth-based former Flight Lieutenant Kuljit Jassal joined the RAAF in 1988, she was the only Sikh woman. And she had to make some adjustments.

"I had long hair, so I got told, 'your hairstyle isn't regulation'," she said.

Kuljit Jassal in 1988 after graduating from Junior Officer Initial Training. ( )

"So I learned to tie a bun!

"Otherwise, it was OK, but there were no other Indians, no other Punjabis."

Ms Jassal said it was gratifying to see so many Sikhs in the ADF today.

"When I joined the military, there was nobody else; I was a trailblazer.

"Now I'm thrilled to see a turbaned soldier."

She said Sikhs have a particular interest in the armed forces.

"Sikhs are known for being a warrior race, a warrior community, and we take pride in defending anything where people are wronged."

Signaller Harshpreet Bachhal joined the army as a way of contributing to society. ( )

Signaller Harshpreet Bachhal's grandfather served with the Indian army, and like many of his faith, he sees joining the military as a way to give back.

"It's sort of instilled in our blood to serve the country that gives you everything," he said.

"That's what my grandfather always told me as well, return your service and give back what our country gave you."

Harshpreet Bachhal's grandfather (far right) was in the Indian military. ( )

Major Amrinder Singh Ghuman was the first Sikh to be commissioned as an officer in the ADF.

"We're a minority community, but the thread of our narrative is etched into the fabric of this nation since World War I," Major Singh said.

"Sikhism is my internal driver … it's the battery from which I derive a lot of my power."

Major Amrinder Singh Ghuman is the highest ranking Sikh in the Australian army. ( )

The latest ADF Census, released in 2023, shows around 90 per cent of the permanent ADF and 80 per cent of the reserves were born in Australia.

Signaller Puran Sandhu, a reservist in Sydney, said the lack of widespread diversity made role models like Major Singh especially important for people from migrant backgrounds.

"At the end of the day, when you see people at a higher rank … it gives you a little bit of hope because it's visible," she said.

"I think the nature of Australia is a melting pot, so you need people of all faiths and backgrounds because it includes diversity of thought."

Signaller Puran Sandhu says Australia's defence forces must be diverse. ( )

Calls to rethink myth of the Anzac soldier

Harjit Singh said he has seen a renewed interest in India's links to Australia's military history.

"The time after World War I was really the peak of the White Australia policy; it wasn't popularised to talk about your brown heritage," he said.

"These days, there are families who've either got a name, like Singh, or have found that their name might have been changed from Singh, who are starting to realise and become proud of that heritage, and they want to know."

He said that was bringing more clarity around who the Anzacs actually were.

"I think there is this sort of myth that's been created about the Australian soldier," he said.

"When people think of that Australian soldier, they usually think of a young white country boy and, while that is absolutely true for the majority of the case, there were men who were brown.

"Just to re-emphasise that in that foundational moment of our country's history, there was a multicultural element to it.

"It wasn't just Sikhs; there were obviously Indigenous people, Chinese Anzacs and others, so it was a multicultural story."

Professor Stanley agreed.

"We have to remember that Anzac Day and Australia is much more diverse than we've traditionally understood," he said.

"It's important for a new, modern, diverse Australia to understand that Anzac Day too has a diverse past."

Professor Peter Stanley says Australians should recognise the diverse history of Anzac Day. ( )

Private Desanda Singh's family had remained in India while he worked in Australia, and while he visited them every few years, he was never able to bring them to Australia permanently, which is why Nechal Singh was born in India.

Nechal said knowing Desanda's history had brought his whole family full circle.

"Prior to me knowing this whole background … Anzac Day was just another day," he said.

"But going and wearing these medals, going to the dawn service, taking my family along, taking my dad along who visited from overseas … it gave me a sense of pride and gratitude.

"Having that sense of connection gave me that whole different sense of belonging.

"I kind of consider myself … even though I'm a first-generation migrant, I'm a fifth- generation Australian."

World.title: 'They deserve death': Officer used police system to monitor wife
World.content:
On the morning of February 23, 2023, Tasmania Police sergeant Chris Cupit logged on to the emergency services internal dispatching system, ESCAD.

But court documents obtained by the ABC show it was not for operational reasons.

WARNING: This article includes details of emotional abuse, intimidation, controlling behaviour and threats of self-harm

It was to keep track of his wife, also a police officer.

He texted her:

Text messages sent by Chris Cupit were read out in the Hobart Magistrates Court. (ABC News/graphic)

It was part of what a presiding magistrate described as the "relentless" monitoring of the victim over a 15-month period — including emotional abuse, intimidation, controlling behaviour, damage to property and threats of self-harm — as detailed in court.

Cupit was arrested on April 30. (Supplied)

In text messages read to the court, Cupit, 42, made repeated threats to kill police colleagues.

He pleaded guilty to one count of emotional abuse or intimidation in the Hobart Magistrates Court and was last year placed on a 12-month community corrections order with 50 hours of community service.

Court hears of 'pattern' of monitoring

Tasmania Police Professional Standards officers analysed Cupit's use of ESCAD, as outlined in court, finding "a pattern" of monitoring the victim's work roster and movements during her shifts.

This included accessing the system from home.

On April 4, 2023, Cupit — who was a sergeant at Bridgewater, north of Hobart — again logged into ESCAD.

"He immediately selected the call sign list, which showed the complainant was partnered with [a constable]," court records state.

The next day, he sent a threat via text message:

"I want to punch that c***"

When the victim was invited to a birthday drink with police colleagues, Cupit made another threat of violence against an officer, as read in court:

Tasmania Police Professional Standards officers found "a pattern" of monitoring the victim's work roster. (ABC News/graphic)

'Those people on your shift are f***ing dead'

In the case facts, read to the court, the mental toll on the victim was clear.

"[She] knew it was not possible for her to keep who she was working with from the defendant due to his access to ESCAD View," court records read.

"[Cupit] demanded the [victim] talk to her sergeant and requested that she only worked with female police officers."

Cupit's conduct continued and escalated throughout 2023, as detailed in a text message he sent to the victim, read to the court:

The mental toll on the victim was clear from the case facts read out in court. (ABC News/graphic)

Other text messages that were read to the court included:

"... I could shoot someone right now" "When I find out who is behind this, I'll f***ing kill them" "Those people on your shift are f***ing dead"

'They deserve death'

On one occasion, Cupit threatened to attend a social gathering and commit violence, text messages show:

Text messages shown in court show Chris Cupit threatened to attend a social gathering and commit violence. (ABC News/graphic)

And threatened to show up at the Hobart Police Station:

"These a**holes need to pay … [they] have it coming" "I hate them so much, I wish death upon them" "They deserve death"

Court documents show he threatened to kill the pet dog he and his wife shared, and damaged property in front of her.

Text messages showed how the victim regularly expressed to Cupit that she feared for her safety.

Cupit was charged with assault and emotional abuse or intimidation in December 2024. (Supplied)

The conduct continued into 2024, including direct threats against police colleagues over the phone.

"[Cupit] said to [the sergeant], 'you're a f***ing dog … you're lucky that we aren't in a room right now, I'd f***ing smash you'," the court was told.

"After the phone call, [Cupit] said to [the victim] that he knew where [the sergeant] lived and he was going to go there."

Cupit was arrested on April 30, and the Professional Standards investigation started. He was charged with assault and emotional abuse or intimidation in December 2024.

Prosecutors chose to tender no evidence on the assault charge, and that charge was dismissed.

Cupit resigned from Tasmania Police.

Victim feared for safety and career

In her victim impact statement, which was read to the court, the victim detailed how she feared for her personal safety, for her career, and how the offending had a lasting impact on herself and her family.

"As someone who has sworn to protect others, I never imagined that I would find myself trapped in a circle of abuse," it reads.

"I have responded to countless family violence incidents in the past, and yet when it was happening to me, I feel powerless.

"I feared that if I spoke out, I would not be believed, that it would jeopardise my career or that I would be seen as weak by my colleagues."

Cupit's defence counsel argued in court that a conviction should not be recorded so that the matter would not impact his ability to obtain registration to work with vulnerable people in the future.

A conviction was recorded, however.

The victim's impact statement was read to the court. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

In sentencing Cupit, Chief Magistrate Catherine Geason referenced another emotional abuse case in saying that "while it does not leave physical marks, it can lead to severe psychological trauma".

Prosecutors did not provide a reason in court for withdrawing the assault charge against Cupit.

Reports from a psychologist and psychiatrist were provided to the court, including Cupit's diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), due to his exposure to traumatic events in his work, exacerbated by diagnosed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

The PTSD was described as "resolved" by the time of sentencing.

"Given your plea of guilty, lack of prior convictions and the impact of the PTSD that you were suffering, the extensive therapy you have engaged in, your remorse and your prospects for the future, I have concluded a sentence other than imprisonment will be appropriate," Ms Geason said.

"The level of emotional abuse and intimidation was significant and a conviction in my view is required to mark the seriousness of the offending."

A family violence order remains in place preventing Cupit from contacting the victim, and not to stalk, threaten, abuse or assault her, among other conditions.

Police information systems policy updated

Tasmania Police reviewed and updated its policy regarding information systems in 2024.

A police spokesperson said this was not due to the Cupit matter but was part of "ongoing organisational improvement".

ESCAD is a dispatching system used by police, fire, ambulance and SES, introduced in 2017.

Serious police officer misconduct allegations increase in Tasmania Allegations of the most serious rated police misconduct have more than doubled in three years, according to police data.

The police spokesperson said that restricting access outside of work hours "may cause unintended consequences" for officers returning to duty outside of rostered hours.

"The policy clearly stipulates members must only access information for work-related purposes and to provide a reason for accessing police or government information systems when required," the spokesperson said.

"All members are required to use their own specific user identification and unique password when logging into police systems."

Officers receive ethical training on the use of police and government information during induction and recruit training.

Professional Standards carries out audits on members' access to information systems, the spokesperson said.

Tasmania Police finalised 45 complaints against officers in 2025 for unauthorised access to information, 43 of which were raised internally.

Breaches of the police code of conduct were found in 24 of the matters, with 13 resulting in verbal guidance for the officer involved.

One officer was reprimanded, another resigned, and one matter was forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, which chose not to proceed with a criminal matter.

World.title: Ancient fossils reveal when the iconic Twelve Apostles formed
World.content:
Victoria's stunning sea stacks known as the Twelve Apostles were carved off coastal cliffs by waves and erosion in only the past few thousand years.

But the geological history of the iconic monoliths, which tower up to 45 metres in height, and of the adjacent coastline goes back millions of years.

It's easy to see in the region's exposed limestone faces, with about 40 kilometres of continuous cliffs that rise to 80m, that ancient marine sediments have been laid on top of each other over time.

Now, a team of geoscientists has narrowed down when the different layers formed over a 16-million-year period, by analysing micro-fossils of sea creatures.

A clear layering of sediments can be seen in the sheer cliff faces of the Port Campbell coastal region. (Supplied: Stephen Gallagher)

Their study, published in Australian Journal of Earth Sciences, provides the most complete picture of the Apostle's geological history so far by combining the findings of previously unpublished research from the 1960s with contemporary fieldwork.

"That is really exciting for two reasons," lead author and micropalaeontologist Stephen Gallagher from the University of Melbourne said.

"Suddenly we know exactly where in Earth history these layers are and we can get a climate record," he said.

"Also, we now know when the whole of the landscape of limestones went from under the sea to land 8.6 million years ago."

What are the Twelve Apostles made of?

The study focused on a 17km stretch from a rock archway, known as The Arch, to Clifton Beach just to the south-east of the Apostles.

Besides shallow clays and sands on the top, most of the cliffs and rocks in this region are made from limestone — which is mostly calcium carbonate remnants of ancient sea life.

And in some areas you can also see an older layer of marl — made from clay and calcium carbonate — above sea level.

Both the limestone and the marl contain microfossils of ancient sea creatures.

Microfossils can be found within the limestone layers of the Twelve Apostles and the region's coastal cliffs. (Supplied: Stephen Gallagher/University of Melbourne)

Dr Gallagher said the largest Apostle contained about 760 trillion microfossils.

"Almost every grain in these limestones is a fossil, basically," he said.

"But you can't see them because they're either microscopic or they've been smashed up."

The time periods when many planktonic microfossils — tiny single-celled organisms with little carbonate shells — existed are well established.

So the identification of each species helped the study's researchers work out when each layer of rock formed.

When did the different layers form?

The rocks that make up the Apostles originally formed in the ocean after Australia made a clean break from Antarctica about 30 million years ago.

As the Australian landmass started drifting northward, from the South Pole, the first layer of the Apostles was forming on a deep sea bed.

Shelly material and clay deposited from about 16 million to 14.1 million years ago became what is known as Gellibrand marl.

Parks Victoria say there are actually just seven limestone stacks on Victoria's southern coast which make up the Twelve Apostles. (Pixabay: xiSerge)

Then the ocean became shallower and a grey limestone layer, the colour coming from some still-present clay, formed up until about 11.6 million years ago.

As the water level became even shallower, a yellow limestone started to deposit.

Around the same time, the continental plate Australia sits on was colliding with the Pacific Plate to the north.

The tectonic shift caused new features, such as the Otway Ranges, to pop up, Dr Gallagher said.

University of Melbourne associate professor Stephen Gallagher using a Jacob's staff to measure the thickness of cliff layers. (Supplied: Mark Cuthell)

This geological activity continued to 8.6 million years ago — indicated by the shallowest layer dated from the yellow limestone — which was when the landmass that would eventually become the Apostles rose from the ocean.

"You [then] had this soil formed on top called the Hesse clay, but there was also sand dunes and some gravel," Dr Gallagher said.

That landmass extended about 40–50km further south than the coastline today.

Curtin University geologist Milo Barham, who was not involved in the study, said the research made a useful contribution by integrating detailed coastal mapping and understanding of the age relationships and rock types along one of Australia's most iconic coastlines.

How did we get the sea stacks that make up the Apostles?

The seven sea stacks known as the Apostles were only formed by erosion in the last 20,000 years or so as ice sheets melted at the end of the last glacial maximum and sea levels rose.

In an area of ocean about 6km from the Twelve Apostles is a feature known as the "Drowned Apostles".

These are five limestone stacks that are thought to be about 60,000 years old, but were quickly swamped by sea level rise.

Further erosion could see the still-standing terrestrial stacks collapse into the waves. But other cliffs will also be turned into new stacks over time.

Before: The Twelve Apostles before the 2005 collapse of a sea stack . . After: and after. (Reuters: Parks Victoria) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE The Twelve Apostles before the 2005 collapse of a sea stack / and after. (Reuters: Parks Victoria)

Matej Lipar, a physical geographer at the Anton Melik Geographical Institute who was not part of the study, said it was important to research the stacks while they still stood.

"Just as scientists are racing to learn from disappearing glaciers, this study is a reminder that limestone stacks are also fragile archives of past environments," he said.

"The Twelve Apostles are not just a tourist attraction, they also preserve millions of years of evidence about changing seas, climates and landscapes."

Dr Gallagher said his next research step would be to work out the climate history of the region in greater detail.

There's only so much time to study the Apostles before they collapse into the ocean. (Pixabay: Stock image)

World.title: Which states get a public holiday for Anzac Day?
World.content:
Anzac Day is coming up on Saturday, but does that mean you get a long weekend?

That depends on where you live and where you work.

When is Anzac Day?

Anzac Day is on April 25 every year.

This year, that date falls on a Saturday.

Is Anzac Day a public holiday?

Yes.

Anzac Day is a public holiday in each state and territory.

When Anzac Day falls on a weekend, many employees are already not working because they have weekends off.

Some state governments decide to observe a public holiday on a weekday, which results in those workers having a day off work.

This year, that bonus day off is on Monday — but that's not Australia-wide.

Which states have a public holiday on Monday?

Only three of Australia's eight states and territories have public holidays on Monday.

The blue jurisdictions on the list below have a public holiday on Monday, the red ones do not.

Yes: ACT The ACT has a public holiday on Saturday and an additional public holiday on Monday. Yes: New South Wales New South Wales has a public holiday on Saturday and an additional public holiday on Monday. No: Northern Territory The Northern Territory has a public holiday on Saturday. It does not have an additional public holiday on Monday. No: Queensland Queensland has a public holiday on Saturday. It does not have an additional public holiday on Monday. No: South Australia South Australia has a public holiday on Saturday. It does not have an additional public holiday on Monday. No: Tasmania Tasmania has a public holiday on Saturday. It does not have an additional public holiday on Monday. No: Victoria Victoria has a public holiday on Saturday. It does not have an additional public holiday on Monday. Yes: Western Australia Western Australia has a public holiday on Saturday and an additional public holiday on Monday.

Source: Fair Work Ombudsman

Does everyone get a long weekend?

Even in the jurisdictions that do have a public holiday on Monday, not everyone will get a day off work.

The Fair Work Ombudsman's website says that, while everyone should be given the choice to work on a public holiday or not, their employers are allowed to request they work on the public holiday — so long as it's a reasonable request.

So people like medical staff and hospitality workers may be rostered on to work despite the public holiday.

Some employees will be paid penalty rates for working on a public holiday, but that depends on what award or agreement they're working under.

You can check out what your entitlements are at the Fair Work website.

Anzac Day is commemorated on April 25. ( )

What about when Anzac Day falls on a Sunday?

Anzac Day will fall on a Sunday next year, which complicates matters even further.

According to the Fair Work Ombudsman's public holiday list for 2027, there are three different options at play for the public holiday across the jurisdictions:

New South Wales and Western Australia will have a public holiday on the Sunday and the Monday .

. The ACT, the Northern Territory and Queensland will have a public holiday on the Monday, but not the Sunday.

but not the Sunday. Tasmania, South Australia and Victoria will only observe a public holiday on the Sunday and will not have a public holiday on the following Monday

Why is Anzac Day on April 25?

It's the anniversary of the first major military action fought by Australian and New Zealand armed forces during World War I.

On April 25, 1915, soldiers landed on the Gallipoli Peninsula, in what was then known as Turkey (which is now officially known as Türkiye).

More than 8,000 Australian soldiers died during the campaign and the military operation had a profound impact on Australians at home.

Why is Anzac Day a public holiday?

It's our national day for honouring people who fought for and aided Australia's armed forces.

You could liken it to Veterans Day in the US or Armed Forces Day in the UK.

While the day is the anniversary of the Gallipoli landing in 1915, it's been broadened out to commemorate the efforts of any Australian in any military action.

So it's not just about people involved in the Gallipoli landing or even World War I, but every military effort.

Anzac Day is an opportunity to honour Australians who served in our armed forces across all military efforts. ( )

How can I find an Anzac Day service near me?

You can find an Anzac Day service near you by checking out the Returned Services League's (RSL) website.

Select your state or territory on the map, click the "filter by" button then type your postcode or suburb in the "filter by location" section.

The website should show you a list of services in locations near you.

World.title: After tornado warnings and midnight matches, Wallaroos are ready for NZ
World.content:
The Wallaroos cannot be blamed if they are relishing the Sunshine Coast's pleasant climate more than most.

Their visit to Queensland comes after they encountered tornado warnings and torrential rain during their two-Test tour of the United States as part of the Pacific Four Series.

Wild weather caused an almost 70-minute delay to the start time of the Wallaroos' 24-0 defeat Canada at a water-logged in Sacramento.

Six days later, when they lost 33-12 to the US in Kansas City, the Australians did not walk off the pitch until well after midnight, with play delayed for two-and-a-half hours due to storms.

At one stage during their stop in Missouri, the players were instructed to move to hallways or stairwells and away from any windows at their hotel as a potential tornado threatened to wreak havoc.

Loading Instagram content

Since arriving back in Australia early Monday morning, the contrast in weather conditions has not gone unnoticed by the Wallaroos.

"It's been great to have nice, clear weather and no tornado warnings," a smiling interim Wallaroos coach Sam Needs said this week.

Lenoard to become Wallaroos' most-capped player Rugby was not on Michaela Leonard's radar when she was a child in Canberra, but she is about to achieve a historic milestone when the Wallaroos meet the Black Ferns on Anzac Day.

As much as they are enjoying the Sunshine Coast, the Wallaroos are not in Queensland for a holiday.

They play trans-Tasman rivals New Zealand in a historic Test at Sunshine Coast Stadium in Kawana Waters on Saturday.

It will be the first time the two teams have met on Anzac Day.

The Wallaroos are more than aware of the daunting task they face, having never beaten the Black Ferns in 29 Tests.

"We've named a big pack, we know New Zealand is going to bring a lot of physicality," Needs said.

"They're going to be strong on both sides of the ball in the collision, and we need to make sure we can match that and try and get over the top of them in that area."

Black Ferns in menacing form

The Black Ferns were also in the US contesting the Pacific Four Series.

The six-time world champions posted a 48-15 win over the hosts in Sacramento and defeated Canada 36-14 in Kansas City.

Comparing the Black Ferns and Wallaroos programs is unfair, as the New Zealanders progressively moved to full-time professionalism during the past decade.

Rugby Australia (RA) is yet to reach that point with the Wallaroos, although — earlier this week — CEO Phil Waugh reiterated a full-time Wallaroos program is one of his organisation's ambitions.

A step forward is RA's guarantee that the Wallaroos will play at least 10 Tests a season in the four-year cycle leading up to the 2029 Women's rugby World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.

The Black Ferns — pictured in their alternate jersey — were undefeated in the US. (Getty images: Ezra Shaw)

Closing the gap in international experience is vital for the Wallaroos, which Needs acknowledged when highlighting the Black Ferns are a Test-hardened unit.

"They've (Black Ferns) got a lot of experience there," Needs said.

"They've got a lot of experience in big games as well."

Needs made several changes to his starting XV to play the Black Ferns in the wake of the loss to the US last Saturday AEST.

Lock Michaela Leonard will play her 46th Test, which will see her become the most-capped player in Wallaroos history.

Lily Bone replaces Emily Chancellor at openside flanker to make her starting debut, while Faitala Moleka has shifted from fullback to fly half.

Waiaria Ellis moves to fullback after being included on the bench against the US.

World.title: Prince Harry delivers messages for Trump, Putin on surprise Ukraine visit
World.content:
WorldEuropePrince Harry Prince Harry delivers messages for Trump, Putin on surprise Ukraine visit David Crowe April 24, 2026 — 5:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

London: Ukraine has gained a $147 billion funding boost to turn back Russian forces after a deadlock over European financial support, as Prince Harry conducts a surprise visit to Kyiv and calls for American leadership to end the war. The new funding comes as Ukrainian leaders harden their message about potential ceasefire terms, with presidential adviser Kyrylo Budanov declaring the country would not give up a “single millimetre” of its territory. Prince Harry at the Kyiv Security Forum on Thursday, after arriving in Ukraine earlier in the day. AP Russian military chief Valery Gerasimov claimed this week that Russia had taken 1700 square kilometres during the fighting so far this year, but expert observers dismissed the estimate and said Ukraine was inflicting significant damage on its enemy. Harry arrived in the Ukrainian capital with no public notice to address the Kyiv Security Forum, where he said he was speaking as a former soldier rather than a political figure.



In a key message to US President Donald Trump and other American leaders, Harry said the US had been part of the assurance offered to Ukraine about its security when it gave up its nuclear weapons after the Cold War, leaving it exposed to Russian aggression today. “This is a moment for American leadership. A moment for America to show that it can honour its international treaty obligations,” he said. “Not out of charity, but out of its enduring role in global security and strategic stability.” Harry has visited Ukraine several times, including visits to medical facilities such as the Superhumans centre in Lviv where soldiers are fitted with prosthetic limbs, given his work with the Invictus Games for soldiers with disabilities. In a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin, the prince said there was “still a moment” to stop the war now and choose a different course.



Russia claims to be succeeding in the war and has gained temporary relief from US sanctions on its oil exports under a controversial decision by the Trump administration last week. “Since the ​beginning of this year, a total of 80 settlements and more than 1700 square kilometres of territory have ​come under our control,” said Valery Gerasimov, chief of the general staff of the Russian forces, in comments reported by Reuters on Tuesday. The Institute for the Study of War, an independent non-profit group, dismissed Gerasimov’s claim as “greatly exaggerated” and said he was probably trying to obscure Russia’s lack of progress. A report by the institute early last month said Russia had occupied 19.4 per cent of Ukrainian territory, compared with 26.8 per cent shortly after the full-scale invasion in February 2022.



“Subsequent Ukrainian counteroffensives left the Russians holding only about 17.9 per cent of Ukraine in November that year,” the institute said of the situation in 2022. Related Article Good Weekend The terrible need that propelled Ukraine to the top of this market “Since then, Russia has seized only 1.5 per cent more Ukrainian land while suffering over one million casualties in total. “Russia has needed three and a half years to seize 9318 square kilometres, an area smaller than Lebanon or Los Angeles County.” The European Union ended months of dispute over funding for Ukraine by reaching a formal agreement in Cyprus on Thursday (late on Wednesday, AEST) to lend the country €90 billion (about $147 billion).



The funding package was decided last year but blocked by Hungarian leader Viktor Orban under rules that required a consensus among leaders. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Welcome to ‘Donnyland’: Ukraine proposes renaming territory in Trump’s honour The election of a new Hungarian prime minister, Peter Magyar, cleared the way for the funds to be released, helped by a Ukrainian decision to resume oil flows from Russia to Hungary through a pipeline across its territory. “We have secured Ukraine’s financial resilience for two years,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky after the formal decision. EU leaders hailed the funding deal as a sign of unity against Russia, with French President Emmanuel Macron talking of a “more sovereign Europe” and Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal warning that peace would not come from compromise with the aggressor.



“We will provide Ukraine what it needs to hold its ground, until Putin understands his war leads nowhere,” said EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas. Related Article Trump diplomacy ‘Throwing Russia lifeline after lifeline’: Latest US backflip delivers another blow to Ukraine Trump sought to negotiate a peace deal with Putin, but the talks have dragged on without any substantial progress on Russia’s demand for large amounts of Ukrainian territory. Budanov, one of Zelensky’s top aides as head of the office of the president, said the negotiation process was sensitive and could not be disclosed, but he indicated there was no compromise on territory. “There will be no acceptance in Ukraine of losing even a single millimetre of our territory,” he told the Kyiv Security Forum.



Prince Harry speaks during a discussion together with Ukrainian war veterans. AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: From six to seven: The big change hitting Victorian number plates
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life From six to seven: The big change hitting Victorian number plates Gemma Grant April 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

In the biggest shake-up to the state’s registration rules in decades, Victorian number plates will soon be able to feature an extra character. Seven-character plates will be on sale for the first time at a “premium auction” in May, where 12 prestigious combinations will be up for grabs. Among the options are 1111111 and AAAAAAA, as well as luxury car brands FERRARI, PORSCHE and MCLAREN, which all conveniently have seven letters. The combination will introduce new possibilities for number plate collectors, like the Fox family. Penny Stephens There will also be a winner’s choice plate available, allowing the highest bidder to select their own seven characters. The changes will eventually expand to the public market at a date yet to be confirmed. Hannah Fox’s family has a long history of collecting number plates that began when her grandfather, billionaire trucking magnate Lindsay Fox, emblazoned his initials on a plate more than 60 years ago.



“For my 18th birthday, I got my initials and my birth year … It’s created a bit of a tradition for the family, everyone kind of has their own little spin on it,” Fox, who works with the Linfox company’s Fox Classic Car Collection museum in the Docklands, said. Of the 12 seven-character plates that will be auctioned next month, Fox has her eye on 8888888 (eight is the family’s lucky number), or would choose CLASSIC as a winner’s choice option. Victoria’s first seven character number plates 1111111

AAAAAAA

MCLAREN

1234567

6666666

PORSCHE

7654321

XXXXXXX

9999999

8888888

FERRARI

Winner’s Choice “It’s bringing in a huge new range of combinations and possibilities,” she said. “It’s probably going to make collecting a bit more accessible … It will be interesting to see what this release of plates will mean in the next 30 or 40 years.”



VicRoads chief executive Giles Thompson said that the new plates were highly sought-after combinations that would pique the interest of eager collectors – particularly given such a major change to the system hasn’t happened in living memory. “Everyone knows the historical combinations that they would have loved, and now’s a chance to get the future combinations,” Thompson said. “Once FERRARI is gone, it’s gone.” Twelve unique seven-character plates will be sold at an auction in May. VicRoads There is already an expensive market for luxury number plates. The handful of single-digit plates are regarded the most desirable, and are generally priced in the millions. The #1 plate is owned by businessman Peter Bartels, and some estimate it to be worth upwards of $10 million. Lindsay Fox was present at its auction, but chose not to outbid his friend Bartels, according to his granddaughter.



Related Article City life Luxury on a plate: Why Victoria’s single-digit rego numbers are worth millions Heritage Only auction house will facilitate the upcoming sales. Owner Ramy Attia said he expected next month’s auction to be dominated by self-made entrepreneurs and successful business owners who were looking to make a statement. “They have already bought everything,” Attia said. “They have the cars, they have the watches, they have the trophy homes.” He said that a rare custom number plate was “like the Rolex for the car”. The unprecedented nature of the new seven character plates means it’s impossible to estimate their value. But Attia is no stranger to eye-watering sales. Eighteen months ago, his company facilitated the sale of plate #24 for just under $2 million.



“Whoever buys these plates, there’s a good chance where you won’t see them transacting in our lifetime … [it] will just get passed down within the family for generations to come,” he said. So what if you’re keen to get your hands on a seven-character plate of your own? Unless you have a small fortune to spare at auction, don’t hold your breath. A public release is unlikely to happen before the end of the year, as internal logistics still need to be sorted. But the change will boost the maximum number of vehicles that can be registered within the state. Car ownership rates across the country are increasing, with many communities reliant on them as a method of transport. “I don’t think we’re close to a [registration] issue with six digits, but … once you get to a seventh, then that becomes a non-issue,” Thompson from VicRoads said. World.title: Is Don, is bad: Don Giovanni a serial abuser not hapless rake
World.content:
CultureTheatreArts Is Don, is bad: Don Giovanni a serial abuser not hapless rake Will Cox April 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

A powerful philanderer brought down by the women he has left in his wake? It could be a newspaper headline. In his 400-year history, the character of Don Giovanni, or Don Juan, has become a folk hero, invariably described as a “trickster”, a “playboy”, and a “seducer”. Mozart saw things differently. This month, Mozart’s 1787 opera, The Rake Punished, or Don Giovanni, returns to the Melbourne stage at the Athenaeum Theatre. Rebecca Rashleigh, who plays Zerlina, and Christopher Tonkin, who plays Don Giovanni, with Suzanne Chaundy, who directs The Rake Punished for Melbourne Opera. Justin McManus “I don’t think Don Giovanni was ever meant to be a hero,” says Suzanne Chaundry, director of The Rake Punished. And yet somehow, over the centuries, he’s become one. Chaundry recalls attending previous productions and seeing audiences delight at the lead character’s charm. “When you actually dig into it, what he’s doing is appalling,” she says. “As soon as you look at it from the woman’s side of things, the opera starts to make a lot more sense.”



Part of Chaundry’s reading of the opera involves restoring its original title, Il dissoluto punito, emphasising the character’s fate. Over the centuries, the name, Don Giovanni, has taken heroic centre-stage. But even the term, “rake”, is easy to read as a loveable rogue, an antihero. The name certainly doesn’t carry connotations of abuse and murder. A poster advertising the opera Don Juan in Seville, Spain. Alamy The opera opens with Giovanni, played by Christopher Tonkin, escaping a woman’s bedroom in disguise. She follows in pursuit. All indications are that “seduction” isn’t the word we would use today. “He’s not averse to using force,” says Chaundry. In his haste to escape, he murders the woman’s father, the Commendatore (Eddie Muliaumaseali’i). Over the course of the opera, his misdeeds pursue him to his grave. The Rake Punished is the latest in a run of Mozart operas for Chaundry, who recently directed productions of The Marriage of Figaro and Così Fan Tutte, also for Melbourne Opera. All three have librettos by Lorenzo Da Ponte.



“Mozart loved women, you know?” says Chaundry. “He was interested in women on a psychological level. His operas often have these really interesting female characters.” In the opera, it’s three female characters, played here by Lee Abrahmsen, Eleanor Greenwood and Rebecca Rashleigh, who drive the Don to his downfall. Through their eyes, he’s seen with a mix of rage, pity and fear. Aside from his charm, he has power and privilege. It’s not hard to see the story through a contemporary lens in an age in which powerful, wealthy men who have used their positions to abuse others are finally held to account. Related Article Arts How this doula uses art to help people take a relaxed look at death The action takes place on stage and off, spilling into the Juliet balconies and beyond. It’s not the only way the piece continues beyond the stage. Chaundry says intimacy co-ordinator Lisa Petty likened the play’s opening scene to many high-profile sexual assault cases in which men are protected by their social and class status. And like countless similar stories brought to light in recent years, Giovanni is a man unburdened by conscience or by consequences.



“It’s absolutely contemporary,” she says. “These themes of power and privilege are so strong.” After the murder, Giovanni is pursued by a previous lover, Donna Elvira, who feels a mix of resentment and pity for him. Giovanni’s servant, Leporello (played by Henry Shaw), recites to her the catalogue of the Don’s conquests – over 2000 women and girls. “We’ve taken a careful approach to staging that catalogue scene, to make sure it really resonates with the audience.” The production gives the women physical presence, using the female chorus. “These aren’t just abstract notions, they’re real people.” Editor's pick Victoria It’s a beloved historic structure, but not even David Attenborough can save Flinders Pier The final character of the trio of women, Zerlina, a peasant whom Giovanni attempts to seduce, is a case in point. “He has this sexual power, and a predatory power, but it’s also that he’s so wealthy,” says Chaundry. “He’s able to offer her, more than anything else, an alternative life.”



It’s complex balance to strike. The opera is a dramma giocoso, a drama comedy, after all, and Chaundry says Giovanni has to be charming, or the women he seduces will look like idiots. But it’s comedy with bite. The story remains focused on the power he has over people. “It’s quite a larrikin production,” says Chaundry. “But we’re careful not to heroicise him.” The Rake Punished is at the Athenaeum Theatre from April 26 to May 3.

World.title: ‘Rents starting to grow’: Bars and restaurants fill city as shop vacancies plummet
World.content:
BusinessMarketsCommercial real estate ‘Rents starting to grow’: Bars and restaurants fill city as shop vacancies plummet Simon Johanson April 24, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

The empty shops that plagued a third of Melbourne’s CBD four to five years ago are now few and far between as vacancy rates plummet and a surge in restaurant and bar openings fills half of the city’s retail space. Shop vacancies in the city centre have fallen steadily from their peak above 30 per cent during the pandemic, and are now sitting at 4.6 per cent, edging down from 6.1 per cent in 2025. Pascal Huron opened his small French casse-croûte in Little Collins Street off Coromandel Place about five months ago. Joe Armao Commercial real estate agency Fitzroys said hospitality, food, beverage and entertainment businesses are the driving interest in street-facing shops, including those in arcades and shopping centres. “Over the past year, the segment increased in representation of the overall tenancy mix to 49.4 per cent,” its latest annual Walk the CBD report states.



The number of empty shops in central Melbourne is now at a long-term low. Swanston Street, which during the pandemic was a minefield of empty storefronts, has a vacancy rate of just 1.9 per cent. Nearby on Little Bourke Street, vacancy has tightened to 1.1 per cent. The long-awaited completion of Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel network spurred leasing activity around the Town Hall and State Library station entrances which disgorge thousands of passengers daily. “Since it’s opened, it’s just absolutely booming around those particular parts of the city,” Fitzroys leasing agent James Lockwood said. Building owners at the top end of Swanston Street near RMIT University are commanding rents around $5000 a square metre. Further south along the street, rents are closer to $3500.



“We’re starting to see those green shoots where rent is starting to increase. It’s a pretty simple supply and demand proposition. There’s less vacancy so, obviously, with more competition rents are starting to grow,” Lockwood said. Chinatown’s vacancy last year was 6.6 per cent. This year, it’s fallen to 3.5 per cent and the appetite from businesses normally wanting to lease in the eastern half of Little Bourke Street is spilling over into Swanston, Russell, Exhibition and Lonsdale streets, he said. Related Article Commercial real estate Squeeze on office space to last beyond 2030 as more workers show up Leasing is strong in Bourke Street Mall. Two upmarket perfume purveyors recently signed in Royal Arcade. Creed Perfume took a 32 square metre space, paying around $3000 per square metre, and luxury French fragrance house Parfums De Marly set up shop in a 61 square metre space for around $2500 per square metre. The rosier retail outlook, however, hasn’t lifted upmarket Collins Street. More shops were empty (6 per cent) on the street that hosts luxury labels like Emporio Armani, Van Cleef & Arpels and Jimmy Choo than the year before. Nearby, in Exhibition Street vacancy was also higher.



Pascal Huron has operated his small French casse-croûte in Little Collins Street off Coromandel Place, selling baguettes to hungry lunchtime workers, for nearly five months. It took him nearly two years to find the right space, a small 17 square metre shopfront. “I wanted to bring a real French casse-croûte to the Paris centre of Melbourne – something small, fast and good quality for the workers around here. I didn’t want a big, expensive cafe. In a small space, I can keep the costs under control. You’ve got less rent, staff, and it’s easier to work,” Huron said. He says city workers are returning to office towers nearby, and generally working more days in the week. “They tend to work three days. Before, a couple of years ago, it was more like one to two days in town,” he said. “I’m getting busier and busier every day, so I’m very happy.” Recent analysis by Bloomberg Intelligence backs Huron’s experience. It shows more than 80 per cent of workers in Sydney and Melbourne are in the office at least three days a week. Occupancy is slowly ticking up, to around 63 per cent at last count, but vacancy in the city’s towers is still historically high at 19 per cent.



Lockwood said retailers are not as reliant on office workers as they were in the past. “It’s a 24/7 CBD,” he said. Traders are now more active midweek and on weekends. “The balance of more people entering the city over Friday nights and the weekends, and their combined spending power, is outweighing the lower visitor numbers being recorded on Mondays and Fridays,” he said. World.title: This mad parrot show might just make Timothee Chalamet think again
World.content:
Elf Lyons: Swan

Factory Theatre, April 22 - 24

★★★★

According to Timothée Chalamet, nobody cares about ballet. Try telling that to British comedian and clown Elf Lyons, who has lovingly created Swan as an accessible guide to the art form, specifically the evergreen Swan Lake.

Seemingly playing a fictionalised version of herself and speaking in a mixture of child-like French and English with purposely mispronounced words, this hybrid of physical comedy and satire is hard to categorise and even harder to resist.

Elf Lyons’ hybrid of physical comedy and satire is hard to resist. asda

Dressed in a parrot outfit concealing a seemingly never-ending array of props and surprises, Lyons makes for an enthusiastic if often bewildered tour guide. Hilariously breaking down the key ballet moves (including the “sexy pair of scissors” and the “Nutribullet”), she explains the most important part of ballet (the curtain calls, of course), reveals why we never see a ballerina over 30 and recreates the most famous dance sequences from Tchaikovsky’s classic with high-kicking fervour.

World.title: ASX set to slide as Wall Street stutters, oil climbs; Meta cuts 8000 jobs; Warner Bros shareholders approve $US110b Paramount deal
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWorld markets ASX set to slide as Wall Street stutters, oil climbs; Meta cuts 8000 jobs; Warner Bros shareholders approve $US110b Paramount deal Stan Choe Updated April 24, 2026 — 5:25am ,first published 1:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

US stocks are pulling back from their record heights on a shaky Wall Street on Thursday following mixed profit reports from Tesla and other big companies. Oil prices, meanwhile, are jumping on worries about what will happen next in the war with Iran. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent, halting a weeks-long rally that had erased all its losses because of the war and then carried it to all-time highs. The Dow Jones was down 240 points, or 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was down 0.9 per cent a day after setting its own record. Wall Street has retreated from its records while oil prices are rising again. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures pointing to a loss of 10 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.6 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was 0.4 per cent lower to US71.35¢ at 5.20am AEST. On Wall Street, Tesla dragged the market lower after falling 3.4 per cent even though it reported better results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on a big jump in Tesla’s forecast for spending this year, as it builds factories to make robots and other products.



“You should expect to see a very significant increase in capital expenditures,” Elon Musk told investors late on Wednesday, “but I think well justified for a substantially increased future revenue stream.” Tech giants Meta (down 2.4 per cent) and Microsoft (down 3.8 per cent) have both taken drastic actions to trim their workforces in an effort to streamline their operations and offset heavy spending on artificial intelligence. Related Article Mergers & acquisitions Trump’s billionaire mate and his son set to win race for Warner Bros after Netflix backs away Meta told personnel in an internal memo that it planned to cut 10 per cent of workers, or roughly 8000 employees, starting on May 20. The social-media company also said it wouldn’t fill 6000 open roles. Earlier in the day, Microsoft issued its own memo offering voluntary buyouts to thousands of its US employees. About 7 per cent of the US workforce will be eligible for the buyouts, according to a person familiar with the planning. The company has never previously done buyouts of this scale, said the person, who requested anonymity to discuss an internal matter. Microsoft had 125,000 employees in the US as of June 2025. That would make about 8750 workers eligible for the program.



Paramount Skydance fell 5.7 per cent after Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders approved selling the business to Paramount. Warner Bros. Discovery slipped 0.7 per cent. Paramount agreed to buy Warner Bros. for $US110 billion ($151 billion) in February, beating out Netflix after a months-long bidding war. Stakeholders are set to receive $US31 in cash for each share of Warner Bros. common stock that they own once the agreement goes through. Shareholders also voted to reject a pay package for Chief Executive Officer David Zaslav. Proxy adviser Institutional Shareholder Services Inc. urged shareholders in April to reject the compensation package, which accelerates equity awards valued at more than $US500 million and includes $US335 million in potential tax reimbursements, calling it “one of the highest golden parachute estimates ever observed.” The vote on pay is nonbinding, however. ServiceNow dropped even more, 17.6 per cent, even though its results for the latest quarter matched analysts’ expectations. The company has been under pressure, along with much of the broad software industry, because of worries that rivals powered by artificial-intelligence technology could undercut its business. In the oil market, prices leaped as uncertainty built about what will happen with the Strait of Hormuz. A ceasefire is still in place between the United States and Iran, but oil tankers aren’t able to get through the narrow waterway off Iran’s coast to exit the Persian Gulf and reach customers.



The US military on Thursday seized another tanker associated with the smuggling of Iranian oil, a day after Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guards took control of two vessels in the strait. President Donald Trump also said Thursday he ordered the U.S. military to “shoot and kill” Iranian boats that deploy mines to gum up traffic in the strait. It’s unclear whether US-Iran peace talks would resume anytime soon. The price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in June rose 3.1 per cent to $US105.06 and at one point topped $US107. That peak coincided with a sudden drawdown for stocks, and the S&P 500 fell as much as 1.3 per cent before it almost as instantly erased half the loss. More expensive oil has hurt airlines in particular because of the industry’s already big fuel bills, and stocks diverged in the industry following the latest profit reports. American Airlines Group rose 1.9 per cent after reporting better profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. American said demand was strong for flights, and it saw the nine best weeks for revenue intake in its 100-year history. Southwest Airlines, though, lost 3.7 per cent after reporting weaker quarterly results than analysts expected. It said it would not give an updated forecast for profit this year because of “the ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty.”



Also on the losing end of Wall Street was IBM, which sank 8.2 per cent despite reporting better profit and revenue for the latest quarter than expected. Investors focused on potentially discouraging numbers underneath the surface, including decelerating growth in trends for its software business. Texas Instruments helped limit Wall Street’s losses after breezing past analysts’ expectations for profit in the latest quarter. CEO Haviv Ilan said the semiconductor company is benefiting from growth led by industrial and data centre customers, and it gave forecasts for profit and revenue in the spring that cleared analysts’ estimates. Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav. Bloomberg The 17.8 per cent leap for Texas Instrument’s stock was the strongest single force pushing upward on the S&P 500. In stock markets abroad, indexes fell across much of Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 0.9 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 0.7 per cent for two of the bigger losses.



South Korea’s Kospi climbed 0.9 per cent after the government reported better-than-expected economic growth for the start of the year, boosted by strong exports, particularly of computer chips used in the AI boom. Semiconductor supplier SK Hynix said its revenue for the latest quarter jumped more than analysts expected largely because of AI-related demand. In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury erased an early dip and rose to 4.31 per cent from 4.30 per cent late Wednesday as oil prices accelerated. A report in the morning said slightly more US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, but the number is still at a historically healthy level. A separate, preliminary report on U.S. business output from S&P Global also suggested growth is improving a bit from its near-stagnation seen in March.
